titleStmt.title: Tractatus de naturis animalium; or, Treatise on the Natures of Animals

sourceDesc.p: Traduction anglaise auto-generee (IA, non relue par un latiniste) a partir du texte latin deja present dans le corpus (edition critique Max Schmitz, 2007, preparee par Isabelle Draelants, encodage XML-TEI par Emmanuelle Kuhry, IRHT). Aucune traduction anglaise, publiee ou du domaine public, de ce traite medieval n'a ete trouvee ; il s'agit donc d'un travail de traduction original. L'oeuvre, redigee vers 1292 a l'abbaye d'Admont, est une compilation de citations d'autorites antiques et medievales (Aristote, Isidore de Seville, Solin, Ambroise de Milan, Pline l'Ancien, et bien d'autres) sur la nature de l'homme (livre I) puis des animaux, organises du general au particulier et classes par mode de locomotion (livre II : quadrupedes marcheurs, serpents, vers, poissons, oiseaux, puis menus volatiles). Chaque entree de la traduction condense, en un paragraphe continu de prose anglaise, les differentes citations que le compilateur medieval avait rassemblees sous une meme rubrique (souvent introduite par "De ..."), en nommant les autorites citees dans le corps du texte plutot qu'en note separee, a l'image de la source latine elle-meme qui attribue chaque citation par un nom d'auteur en marge. Les reperes entre crochets (ex. "[II, 2, 1, 2]") reprennent la numerotation livre/section de l'edition critique et permettent de recouper avec le texte latin. Traduction fournie a titre de meilleur effort ; a verifier par un latiniste avant toute citation savante.

div.head: Who has written on the natures of animals [Prologue]
div.p: Many have written on the natures of animals, not only in various manners but also from different motives and occasions. Some, as philosophers, investigating the natures and properties of things through their causes, set forth the diversity of animal natures - both in temperament and in the composition of their bodily parts - as useful rules drawn from the necessary principles of natural science; they likewise gathered, by subtler and higher speculation, the diversities of all their behaviours, habits and customs into similarly universal rules. In this way Aristotle wrote on the natures of animals in his book called On Animals, and attempted still more of the same in his Natural History. Others, not contemplating these things as philosophers but wishing, as historians and observers, to report new and unusual things for the delight of their readers, wrote various things about the natures of animals - that is, about their habits and customary doings - not rendering the cause of each but rather narrating something as if it were a marvel; in this way wrote Solinus and Jacobus [of Vitry]. Hence Solinus first called his book, whose title he later changed, a Collection of Memorable Things. Still others, not investigating causes as philosophers do, nor intending to relate marvels as observers and historians do, but for the sake of words - that is, of interpreting the names of individual things - touched on something of the natures of animals, as Isidore did in his book of Etymologies, and others who wrote on the etymologies of names. They also kept different orders: for the philosophers and historians spoke of natures - that is, of the habits of animals - not in continuous narration but scattered here and there, while the etymologists, looking more to the order of words than of things, wrote according to the sequence of vocabulary. Blessed Ambrose too, in his book the Hexaemeron, touches on the natures of certain animals as if in passing, and so do other Catholic writers. All of these, taken together, not only advanced the knowledge of the natures of animals but also served no small measure the delight found in hearing and perceiving marvellous things, so that reading of this kind is not only useful to students but also pleasant and agreeable even to the weary - provided that what is said is confirmed by the authority and testimony of the ancients. For, as Solinus says, we can bring forward almost nothing new of our own, since the diligence of the ancients has left nothing untried.

div.head: [I, 1, 1] On menstruation
div.p: As the natural philosopher Democritus says, woman alone among animals is a menstrual creature; but according to Aristotle this must be understood to mean that the females of other animals also menstruate, though not so often nor so visibly. Solinus says that the menstrual flow is, as it were, a monstrous thing because of its remarkable effects: crops touched by menstruating women will not sprout, must turns sour, grasses touched by them die, trees lose their fruit, iron rusts, and all bronze blackens; if dogs happen to taste of it they are driven mad with a rage that no iron can restrain, and it even breaks the bitumen - very strong and sticky - that forms in the lake of Judea called Asphaltites; all this it does because of the great natural heat it contains. Hence too, as Aristotle says, some suppose woman to be hotter than man - which is not true; her only useful property in this regard is that the star of Helen, most hostile to sailors, is tempered by it. Whence the poet: "Sad to those borne on the sea is the sight of Helen among the stars." Likewise, as Aristotle says in his book On Sleep and Waking, if a woman looks into a mirror during her menstrual time, the surface of the mirror becomes as it were a bloody cloud, and if the mirror is new this stain is difficult to wipe away. Isidore says the word menstruum comes from mensis (month), because this flow customarily occurs naturally after the cycle of the lunar month; he adds that after several such monthly days the seed [that would follow] cannot generate, because according to Isidore the menstrual blood is itself the matter of seed. Solinus also relates that a certain woman bore four twins in a single birth, and that in Egypt, on account of the fertilizing power of the waters of the Nile, women sometimes bear seven sons at once - though Aristotle says a woman cannot conceive more than four at a time. Also, as Solinus says, women bear children up to the fiftieth year, men beget up to the eightieth and beyond. And, as Solinus says, above all women who intend to conceive must beware of sneezing after intercourse; and if they have conceived, by the tenth day the head and feet will already be discernible, after which they begin to feel the weight of pregnancy, their sight grows weaker, and their usual appetite for food ceases.

div.head: [I, 1, 2] On the signs of conceiving a male or a female
div.p: The signs of having conceived a male or a female are, according to Solinus, these: if it is a male, pregnant women have a better complexion and an easier delivery, and the male begins to move in the womb on the fortieth day, the female on the ninetieth; but if it is a female, pregnant women have a pale complexion, heavy and sluggish legs, and a harder delivery.

div.head: [I, 1, 3] On the manner of the embryo's formation
div.p: The manner of the conception and formation of the embryo is, according to Solinus and Isidore, as follows: from the woman there is first formed a kind of flesh in the shape of a cord, and then, over an interval of time and days, the other members are distinguished; thus it grows and takes shape in the womb, and from the day of conception it is nourished for the remaining eighty days until birth. A gloss on the verse "in forty-six years was this temple built" says that the seed received into the womb has, for the first six days, the likeness of milk; then over nine days it turns into a form of blood; then over twelve days a kind of flesh is formed from it; then over eighteen days that flesh is distinguished into limbs, in every feature and shape, and thereafter the conceived child grows and is nourished until birth. Hence the verses: "Believe that the seed is conceived in the first six days; it becomes as it were milk, and in the next nine it becomes blood; then for twice six plus nine days more it consolidates and takes shape, and the time that follows brings it to birth."

div.head: [I, 1, 4] Which member is formed first
div.p: Aristotle says that in blooded animals the heart is the first member formed in the process of creation. Isidore, however, says that the head is formed first among the rest, and proves this from eggs, in which unfinished chicks are found that appear to have a head and the openings of the eyes before any other member. Certain physicians hold that the brain is the first member universally created; yet the inner members are created before the outer, and the principal before the secondary and auxiliary ones, and from this Aristotle's view appears the better. In both sexes, as Solinus says, when the hair begins to grow the pain of childbirth increases the more; and pregnant women suffer more at the full moon, and those born at the full moon are weaker and have a moister brain - though Aristotle says the contrary, that nights of the full moon are hotter, and accordingly those born then would not have a moister brain than others. When a pregnant woman eats overly salted food, her child, as Solinus says, is usually born without nails, from which it appears that the growth of nails comes from a sweet, viscous phlegm. Likewise, so that a woman may give birth easily, she should, as far as she can, hold her breath during labour, as Solinus says, because the expulsive power and the loosening of the embryo's attachment to the womb are strengthened by the retention of breath, as is seen in those who are constipated and strain to relieve themselves through this same aid. Also, as Solinus says, it is against nature for a child to come forth from the womb feet first; such children are for this reason called Agrippae ("born in difficulty"), and it is a sign of misfortune for those so born. Some, too, are born only by the cutting open of their mothers, as was Scipio Africanus who, as Solinus says, was for this reason the first of the Romans to be called Caesar, from caesus, "cut," referring to his mother's womb. Also, as Solinus says, many oddities have been observed among newborns: some have been seen born with teeth, as Gnaeus Pompeius, who was for this reason surnamed "Toothy"; others have had, instead of individual teeth, one continuous bone in place of them, as did the son of Prusias, king of Bithynia. Men generally have more teeth than women. Also, those whose canine teeth (called cynodontes) appear first on the right side will be fortunate and happy, while those on the left will have the opposite fate. The first sound of a newborn, Solinus says, is crying, and infants do not naturally laugh before the fortieth day; Crassus, the great-grandfather of Socrates, is said never to have laughed at all, whereas Socrates himself laughed in the very first hour of his birth, which is said to be a sign of good fortune. Hence Virgil in the Georgics: "Begin, little boy, to know your mother by your smile," and so on.

div.head: [I, 1, 5] On the unchangeableness of certain men's faces
div.p: Solinus relates that certain men have always kept the very same cast of countenance, as Socrates, Heraclitus and Diogenes; that others have never been seen to laugh, nor even to belch, as the poet Pomponius; that others, such as one nicknamed Antonius Andrusus, are said never to have spat. Some are also recorded, as the same Solinus says, to have been born with their bones already hardened, and never in their lives to have sweated or thirsted, as Ligdamus of Syracuse, whose bones, when found, were said to contain no marrow.

div.head: [I, 1, 6-7] On strength and stature
div.p: The strength of animals and of men lies wholly in the sinews, which are the stronger the denser and more continuous they are. Solinus tells of a certain gladiator, Tritannus, who in combat and in boxing could strike backward with his arms as forcefully as forward. Solinus also says that the eagle-stone (allectorius), which is found in the crop of a cock, once the cock has been castrated, brings victory and strength to fighters who carry it. Of the striking resemblance of face and countenance found among many people, Solinus says that this trait has been observed not only among blood relations of the same family but even among strangers, so much so that a certain Artemon so closely resembled Antiochus, king of Syria, that when Antiochus died, his own son, through the scheming of his mother who arranged the likeness, was made to succeed to the kingdom in Artemon's place. As for the measure of bodily stature, Solinus says that a man's height, from heel to crown, equals the span between the fingertips of his two hands when the arms are stretched out - which is why, on account of this roundness of figure, physicians have called man "the lesser world," whence the Greek term microcosmus, "smaller world." Some say that no man exceeds seven feet in height, but according to Solinus the contrary has often been observed: he reports that the bones of Orestes, found by the Spartans at Tegea, measured seven cubits, and that in Scripture giants of the line of Anak are named, such as that Goliath in the Book of Kings. Solinus also tells of a boy at Salamis who grew three cubits in three years, but who thereafter, as he grew older, remained weak and infirm until his death.

div.head: [I, 1, 8] On speed
div.p: The right side of the body, as Solinus says, moves more readily, on account of the spreading extension of the sinews and veins proceeding from the heart, whose extension on the left is more constricted because of its nearness to the point of the heart from which they arise; the left side, however, is stronger, and for this reason nature ordained the left side, as it were, for bearing burdens, and the right for movement and gesture. Hippocrates says that no woman is naturally ambidextrous. Speed of movement comes from an abundance of heat and its intensity. Solinus tells of a man so swift that he outran a hare in a race, and of another who covered seventy-five miles between noon and evening.

div.head: [I, 1, 9] On skill and dexterity
div.p: Cicero, as Solinus says, was so skilled that he wrote the whole history of Troy so minutely on parchment that it could be enclosed within a nutshell - though I think this doubtful. Likewise a certain craftsman, as the same author reports, carved ants out of ivory so finely that they could scarcely be told apart from real ants.

div.head: [I, 1, 10] On keenness of sight
div.p: Keenness of sight comes from the strength of the visual spirit in the brain and the fineness of the crystalline humour and of the membrane covering the eye. Sight is deceived in two ways, as Aristotle says in his book On Sleep and Waking: in one way, when the sense is moved while the sensible object is not moved, as it appears to those on a ship that the mountains and shore are moving past on either side; in the second way, when the visual rays and spirits are interrupted, as when someone presses the pupil of the eye out of its place, so that one object seems to be two, as happens to the cross-eyed, and as when, with the fingers crossed, some small round object such as wax or a bean is touched, it will seem that there are two. There are many kinds of distorted and indirect vision. Whence the verse: "The squint-eyed sees aslant but sees the heights truly; the sharp-sighted sees things nearby, the bleary-eyed grows moist." Solinus says that a certain man had such power of sight that from a watchtower at Lilybaeum in Sicily he saw the fleet setting out from Carthage in Africa and counted the whole number of men aboard the ships. The same author reports that in Scythia there are women called the Bithyae who have two pupils in their eyes, and who, if they look upon someone in anger, kill by their gaze alone; the like are found in Sardinia.

div.head: [I, 1, 11] On the chambers of the head
div.p: The chambers of the human head, or brain, are three: the front one, called the imaginative; the middle one, called the intellectual or discerning; and the rear one, called the chamber of memory. The first is warmer and moister, the middle warmer and drier, the last colder and drier - for these qualities suit their respective functions: from heat comes quickness of apprehension, from moisture aptitude for receiving, and from dryness and cold firmness of retention.

div.head: [I, 1, 12] On memory
div.p: Solinus relates that a certain envoy of King Pyrrhus had such power of memory that on the second day after entering Rome he greeted, by their own proper names, the entire Senate and the whole order of knights, whose names he had learned only the day before. The same author says that the philosopher Metrodorus had such memory that he retained instantly, in their exact order of words and sense, everything said or read to him.

div.head: [I, 1, 13] On the loss of memory
div.p: Memory, as Solinus says, is lost in three ways: through fear, through accident, and through disease. He relates that a certain man, having received a wound to the back of his head, fell into such forgetfulness that he no longer knew his own name; fear and terror indeed destroy memory, but they can also provoke voice and speech even in the mute. Solinus tells how the mute son of King Croesus, when Cyrus had entered the town of Sardis where Croesus then lay hidden, suddenly burst into speech, crying: "Spare my father, Cyrus, and learn even from our misfortunes that you too are but a man."

div.head: [I, 1, 14] On the natural gentleness in man
div.p: Man is by nature a gentle animal, as Aristotle says, and this is to be understood in that he alone has, of himself, the art and instructor of gentleness - namely, the rational soul; other animals grow tame not by nature but by training and effort, and for this reason nature did not give man limbs for fighting on his own, such as sharp teeth or horns. Among all animals man has, in proportion to the size of his body, the smallest mouth, as Aristotle says; by this nature meant to teach man moderation in the offices of the mouth, that is, in eating and in speaking. Likewise all animals walk with their bodies bent toward the ground, and man alone stands upright; this is, as Aristotle says, because of the abundance of blood in man's upper part, and because it was fitting for a rational creature to look toward heaven rather than toward earth. Whence Ovid: "While the other animals look down and gaze at the earth, he gave man a face held high and bade him look upon the sky and lift his upright countenance to the stars."

div.head: [I, 1, 14, note] Various curiosities of the human body
div.p: Pythagoras says that from the spine of a dead man a serpent may be generated. Solinus also says that nature has so far distinguished modesty even among dead bodies that when the corpses of the drowned are cast up by the waves, the bodies of women float face down, but those of men face up. Some say that man is surpassed by certain kinds of animals in certain of the senses; hence the saying: "The boar surpasses us in hearing, the lynx in sight, the ape in taste, the vulture in smell, the spider in touch." But Aristotle says the contrary in his book On the Soul, that man has, of all animals, the poorest sense of smell, but has more of the sense of touch than any other animal; it is true, however, that the spider surpasses man in touch as regards the fineness of what is touched, though not as regards the [overall] sense of touching. Likewise, as Aristotle says, no animal has as many inner and outer members as man, and this is because of the great number of his operations and the perfection of his nature, since he is the most perfect of all animals. For the rest concerning the nature of man, the composition of his body, the manner of generation, and all his inner and outer members, one should consult Aristotle's book On Animals; what has been set down here from the other authors shall suffice as excerpts.

div.head: [I, 1, 15] On the stages of life
div.p: The stages of human life are, according to Isidore, six: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age. Others, such as certain physicians, count only four stages: infancy, adolescence, youth, and old age. According to Isidore, these are the boundaries of the six ages: infancy lasts from the day of birth to the seventh year, and is called infantia from the privation of fari, that is, of speaking. Childhood (pueritia) lasts to the fourteenth year, and is so called from purity (puritas), because up to that time children are pure of intercourse, being as yet unable to beget. Adolescence extends to the twenty-ninth year, and is named from adolescere, that is, from growing, because up to that limit the body continues to grow, and meanwhile they are already fit for intercourse - though Aristotle says that every animal grows, in the first half of its life, to reach its full growth. Youth then lasts to the fiftieth year, in which is the completion of all strength and growth, whence it is named from iuvamentum, "help" or "benefit." Then follows gravitas, maturity, which is the decline of youth toward old age, lasting to the seventieth year, so named because the body already begins to grow heavy. The last stage is old age, from the seventieth year to the end. Those who reckon four ages base this on four temperaments: the body is first hot and moist, and this is infancy; then hot and dry, adolescence; then cold and moist, youth; then cold and dry, old age. And so Aristotle says, in his book On Life and Death, that old age stands opposite to infancy, since the beginning of life, as in infants, is hot and moist, while its privation in the old is cold and dry; these are contraries, and there is no passage from one contrary to another except through all the intermediate states between them, as Aristotle says in the seventh book of the Physics; hence the middle ages must be hot-and-dry and cold-and-moist, that is, adolescence and youth, by whatever names they are called. Those who set out six ages, such as Isidore, had regard to the movement of decline from the first age to the second and from the third to the fourth, and so placed childhood between infancy and adolescence, and maturity between youth and old age; but between the middle ages themselves they placed no further intermediate stage - that is, between adolescence and youth - because, owing to their similar temperance, the passage between them without any further intermediate seemed easier. Character, too, naturally varies according to the stages of life, as Horace shows in his Art of Poetry, speaking first of boys: "The boy who can already speak clearly and set his foot firmly on the ground longs to play with his fellows, conceives and abandons anger on a whim, and changes by the hour"; and of young men: "The beardless youth, his guardian at last removed, delights in horses and hounds and the grass of the sunny Campus; pliable as wax to be bent toward vice, harsh toward those who admonish him, slow to provide for what is useful, prodigal of money, lofty and eager, and quick to abandon what he has loved."

div.head: [I, 1, 16] On grown men and on old men
div.p: Horace continues: "The grown man's pursuits and temper seek different things: he pursues wealth and friendships, he serves ambition, and is wary of committing himself to what he might soon have to change." And of old men: "Many troubles beset the old man: either he seeks gain and, having found it, wretchedly abstains from using it and fears to enjoy it; or he manages all his affairs timidly and coldly, a procrastinator, slow to hope, sluggish, and yet greedy for the future; difficult, querulous, a praiser of times past when he was a boy, and a censor and critic of the young." Character likewise varies according to bodily temperament:

div.head: [I, 1, 17-20] The four temperaments
div.p: Of the sanguine man the verse says: "generous, loving, cheerful, laughing, ruddy of complexion, fond of singing, well-fleshed, easily satisfied, bold, and kindly." Of the choleric man: "cunning, deceitful, vengeful, prodigal, bold, shaggy, lean, dry, and of a saffron complexion." Of the phlegmatic man: "sleepy, sluggish, much given to spitting, dull of sense, with a fleshy face and a pale complexion." Of the melancholic man: "envious and sad, covetous, tenacious with his right hand, not without deceit, timid, and of a muddy complexion." And it must be noted that a man's natural temperament can be changed into its opposite, sometimes by teaching and habit, sometimes by grace, which also bends man's free will toward the better.

div.head: [I, 1, 21] On the sexes
div.p: Men also differ naturally among themselves by sex, namely male and female. Male and female, as Aristotle holds, differ as efficient cause and matter; they differ also in the members by which sex is distinguished in animals, and in temperament, since the male is hotter and drier, the female colder and moister - whence it is said that the hottest woman is colder than the coldest man. They differ also, as Aristotle and Isidore say, in bodily size and strength, since in every kind of animal the female is of weaker and smaller body. They differ likewise in natural character: the masculine temper, as Aristotle says in his Physiognomy, is vehement, quick to impulse, unmindful of grudges, generous in living according to virtue, studious and magnanimous; the feminine temper, however, is cunning, prone to anger, tenacious of grudges, merciless, envious, impatient of labour, docile, sly, flattering, hasty, timid, and ingenious in wicked doings. A gloss on the verse "her strength is in her loins" says that lust resides in men in the loins and in women in the navel, and this is true, since according to Aristotle's book On Animals the passages through which seed is conveyed in men are the loins and kidneys, while in women it is a vein proceeding from the head to the navel, which there contains the womb. For the rest concerning the difference between the sexes, one should consult the book On Animals and Aristotle's Physiognomy.

div.head: [I, 2, 1] On the monstrous races of mankind
div.p: As Aristotle testifies in the third book of the Physics, monsters are, in nature, its faults and errors, occurring when nature happens to err by way of accident, so that offspring unlike its parents in kind or in shape or form is produced. The accident by which nature is impeded is threefold, as Aristotle indicates in his book On Animals: first, excessive weakness of the operative power and of the descending seed, from which follows a dissimilarity in kind, as when a man begets a bull, or a man having the head of a bull, so that the likeness between the begotten and the begetter holds only according to genus, not according to individual or species, because of the weakness of the power; second, a diminishment of that same power, as when someone is born lacking a limb - without a hand, or a foot, or a head; third, an excess of the temperament, whereby a man may be born with six fingers on one hand, or with two heads - and this excess or deficiency may occur either in the essential members or in the accessory ones, so that in sum there are three kinds of monsters: those arising through a change into a contrary species, those through a diminishment of members, and those through an excess of them. There is a difference, as Isidore says, between a "monster" and a "portent": monsters are those which, differing from the common form of mankind, derive their origin from themselves according to an inveterate pattern of error - whether through great bodily size, as giants born of giants, or through smallness, as pygmies born of pygmies, or through some transformation, excess, or deficiency of limbs, as the dog-headed men, the two-headed, the three-handed, and those with double rows of teeth (called by the Greeks steresioi, meaning those lacking a head or hands and feet). Portents, however, are those which are generated, by accident, from natural animals or men contrary to the usual course of nature - as Isidore relates that in the time of King Xerxes a fox was born of a mare, and that in the time of Alexander the Great a monster was born of a woman whose upper body was human, though dead, and whose lower body was that of a beast, and living; and these are called portenta, "portents," from portendere, "to foretell," because they always seem to signify something, such as a change of king or kingdom. Such beings, as Aristotle says, do not live long but die at once, because nature erred in their creation and their principal members are weak. But concerning those monstrous races that persist and have a fixed span of life, and their own regions which they inhabit and in which they reproduce themselves, as Isidore and Solinus write - it is doubtful whence they take their origin. For either they take their first principle and origin from natural men through some error of nature and by way of accident, or else one must grant that they are another race of men not descended from Adam but derived from some other first parent; but this is unfitting to grant, since it is impossible that there were two first men, nor is it fitting that many should have been created at once. For this reason, according to the opinion of some, it may be answered that such monsters first took their origin from natural men, nature having erred; but how that race of monsters was afterward propagated among themselves - the dog-headed, the three-handed and the like - so that they came to possess their own regions and places of habitation, as Solinus reports such monsters to exist in India, seems doubtful in view of Aristotle's statement that such monsters are short-lived and imperfect; for if they are short-lived and imperfect, it seems strange how they could reproduce and multiply so as to occupy their own territories among the nations. To this it may be answered that, although such monsters first took their principle and origin from natural men through an error of nature, they were afterward so confirmed that they then bred true among themselves; the cause of this seems to lie in the nature and quality of the places in which such monsters were first generated or to which they came - such as the mountains of India, Libya, and Scythia, for these lands are the nurseries of monstrous men and other animals - and the first principle in this appears to be the action of the heavens and the influence of the higher bodies, in the same way that in Ethiopia men are black and in the northern region white; for the power of the heavens seems able to produce the same effect there, in the transformation, diminishment or excess of limbs, as it produces in Ethiopians and Gauls in the matter of the diversity of their colour.

div.head: [I, 2, 2] On the kinds of monsters
div.p: The kinds of monsters are uncertain, nor is it necessary to seek out their differences and precise classification, just as in moral matters one need not seek out the species of evil, but only of virtue and good; for the mean in moral matters is one and fixed, while deviations from the mean are infinite - so too in nature the species and genera, so far as they concern the completion and perfection of nature and its operation, are in some sense finite and fixed, while its deviations and errors are infinite; for this reason it is not necessary to seek fixed genera of monsters and the like. Those which have, however, been described and named by the authorities, are, by way of example, these: giants (gigantes) are so named, according to Isidore, as though gegines, that is, "earth-born" - for ge in Greek means "earth" - and they are men who surpass others in bulk and size, as that Goliath in the Book of Kings, and of whom it is said in Genesis that there were giants upon the earth in those days. According to the fables, giants are called sons of the earth because in their bulk and size they resembled the earth, such as Tityos, a giant lying across eight acres of ground, and Antaeus, and Ixion, and others like them. Pygmies, or dwarfs, are certain little men dwelling in the mountains of India near the shores of the ocean, measuring one cubit. These, as Solinus says, build their houses of reeds and papyrus and live communally on the hunting of sea-fish and other small creatures; they wage constant war against cranes. Of them it is said in Ezekiel: "the Pygmy race is in your towers," and so on. The Cynocephali ("dog-heads") are so called because they have, on human bodies, the heads of dogs - kynos in Greek meaning "dog," kephale "head"; these bark like dogs and feed on the raw flesh they hunt, and they are born in India also. The Cyclopes are so named because they have a single eye in the middle of the forehead; they are also called agriophagitae, "eaters of wild things," for they eat only wild beasts - agrios in Greek meaning "wild," phagein "to eat." According to the fables they were, as Solinus says, the forgers of Jupiter's thunderbolts, dwelling in Sicily near Mount Etna, according to the line: "the Cyclopes forging thunderbolts at Jove's command." Isidore, however, says these exist only in India. The Lemniae, as Solinus reports, are said to exist in Libya without heads, having mouth and eyes in their chest; elsewhere others are born without necks, having eyes and ears on their shoulders. In the farthest parts of the East, as Solinus writes, there are many monstrous races: some are there without nostrils, with very wide mouths and misshapen faces; others have a lower lip so prominent that in sleeping they cover their whole face with it against the heat of the sun; others still lack a mouth altogether and have in its place only a small opening through which they merely suck the juices of reeds and papyrus, living on that alone; and some there have no tongues, and use nods or gestures instead of speech to make known their wishes to one another. Among the Scythians there are certain people called the Panotii, having ears so broad and spread out that in rain and in heat they cover their whole body with them - named from the Greek pan, "all," and ous/otos, "ear." In Ethiopia there are those called the Artabatitae, who walk bent forward like beasts, and none of them lives beyond forty years. The Satyrs, according to Isidore, are certain little men with hooked noses, horns on their foreheads, and goat's feet - such a one Saint Anthony saw in the desert, as blessed Jerome writes, who, on being questioned by him, is said to have answered: "I am a mortal, one of the inhabitants of the desert, whom the pagans, deluded by various error, worship as fauns and satyrs." There are also other wild men, whom some call fig-fauns (faunos ficarios). The Sciapods are in Ethiopia, having feet so broad that lying on their backs on the ground they cover their whole body with them against the heat, but each of them has only a single foot, and yet they are extremely swift runners. The Antipodes are in Libya, men having their soles turned backward and eight toes on each foot. Also in Scythia there are men having horse's feet, as Isidore says, called Hippopodes according to the fables. The Centaurs were such creatures, having the hindquarters in the form of a horse; but this is to be understood historically, since Thessaly was the homeland of the Centaurs, where the practice of taming and riding horses was first discovered, as Solinus says, and so the fable makes Chiron, the tutor of Achilles, a Centaur and king of Thessaly. Also in India, as Isidore says, there is a certain race of women who conceive in their fifth year and do not live beyond their eighth. In Scythia there are men called Essedones, that is anthropophagi, "eaters of men": these feed on nothing but human flesh, as Solinus says - from the Greek anthropos, "man," and phagein, "to eat." Augustine, in his book The City of God, says that just as among the whole community of nations there are certain monstrous men, so too among the whole community of men there are certain monstrous nations - meaning by this that not only are those now named monsters truly monstrous, but that, throughout the whole community of natural men and nations, however many diversities of custom there are, there are in some sense that many kinds of monsters. For the rest concerning the diversity of monstrous races, one should consult Solinus.

div.head: [II, 1, 1] Definition of animal
div.p: An animal, as Porphyry says, is an animate, sentient body. "Body" is set down as its genus; "animate" as its matter; "sentient" as its specific difference, distinguishing it from inanimate bodies such as stones and clods and the like. "Sentient" is set down to distinguish it from plants, which are likewise animate bodies, since they grow and live, but do not have sensation. Now "sentient," in the proper sense of an animal, refers to the sense of touch, because, as Aristotle says in his book On the Soul, touch alone makes an animal to be an animal; the other four senses exist in animals for their well-being.

div.head: [II, 1, 2] The division of animal
div.p: "Animal" is divided in two ways: according to matter and according to form. According to form it is divided into rational and irrational. The rational is that already spoken of [man]; the irrational includes the lion, the goat, and all animals other than man. According to matter, however, the kinds of animals are divided in many ways: into quadrupeds and bipeds; into walking, flying and aquatic creatures; into stag, lion and wolf; these divisions will become clearer later.

div.head: [II, 1, 3] Two questions
div.p: A question arises here: first, whether the rational animal, man, is one in species and admits of no further subdivision, while the irrational - which stands as its collateral opposite - does subdivide; and second, whether irrational animals differ from one another in species, as do the lion, the stag and the wolf. To the first question it must be said that, according to some, man is undivided and one in species, because the human body, in relation to all other animals, is equal and most temperate, standing as it were at the mean. The mean is always one and undivided, and every equality, as Boethius says in his Arithmetic, is scant and finite, whereas inequality is numerous and manifold; other animals, however, multiply in species according to the diverse degrees of their departure from the temperate mean - as the lion is hot and dry, the ass cold and dry; land animals tend to be hotter and drier, aquatic animals moister and colder, flying creatures hotter and moister. As to whether these differences, being material, produce a diversity of species among irrational animals, as was asked - this seems difficult to grant, since specific differences ought to be taken from form and not from matter. Averroes too, in his commentary on the first book On the Soul, says that the limbs of the stag and the lion differ not in matter but in form; but what is meant here by "form" or "matter" is left to further discussion.

div.head: [II, 1, 4] On the kinds of animals
div.p: The division of animals proceeds in many ways. They may be divided according to the elements and places in which they live, some being terrestrial, some aquatic, and some aerial, called flying creatures; some, as Ambrose says, are amphibious (amphygena), living at once in water and on land, such as the crocodile, the hippopotamus and the beaver. Terrestrial creatures are further subdivided into walking and creeping ones, although many creeping creatures too are amphibious - that is, living in different elements - such as the water-snake and the eel. Walking creatures are all those that go about on feet; creeping creatures, however, are those that contract and extend themselves by certain ring-like joints of the spine, and by this motion do not walk but crawl, as serpents do. Sometimes, as Ambrose and Isidore say, the whole class of creeping things is called by the name "serpent," from serpere, "to crawl." Aristotle says that the difference between creeping and walking creatures is that walking creatures have blood and are warmer, whereas all creeping creatures lack blood, are cold, and are for this reason venomous.

div.head: [II, 1, 4, note] General rules concerning animals
div.p: The use of locomotion, as Aristotle says, is the pursuit of food. Creeping creatures, however, have their food readily at hand, since they feed on earth; and some animals altogether lack the power of forward motion, being those whose food is always present to them, such as sea-snails and shellfish. Every bloodless animal lacks a heart and lungs, and every animal lacking lungs lacks a voice. Every bloodless animal has something in place of blood. Every animal possessing a heart has it in the middle of its body, except man. Every blooded animal has a liver. Every animal possessing all the senses has a head. Every animal sleeps and wakes, though some longer, some more briefly. Every sleeping creature closes its eyes, except the lion and the hare. Every animal that has eyes has them, as Ambrose says, set higher in the head than does man. Every animal that has ears moves them, except man. Every animal that has horns has them hollow, except the stag. Every animal that has a tail lacks buttocks, and every animal that has buttocks lacks a tail. Every animal that lives by plunder has sharp and strong teeth. Every walking animal has an equal number of feet on each side, so that its body is equally free to move on either side, lest it be lighter for motion on one side and heavier on the other. Every animal with sharp claws, as Pliny says, gives birth with difficulty.

div.head: [II, 1, 4, note 2] Further general rules
div.p: Every sick animal is cured, as Ambrose says, by drinking dog's blood. Every large-bodied animal reproduces sparingly. Every animal with many toes on its feet begets young that are born blind. Every animal, except man, mates only at a fixed season. Domestic animals mate more often than wild ones. All wild animals grow tame once they have had abundant food. For the rest of the general rules, one should consult Aristotle's book On Animals; our present intention here concerns only the particular kinds.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 1] On walking animals
div.p: Of walking animals, some are four-footed, some two-footed, some many-footed. Of all these, some are domestic, some wild; some fierce, some tame; some live by plunder, others by labour; some eat flesh, others grass and herbage. Now all those that eat grass have longer necks than those that eat flesh, as Ambrose says, and these latter have teeth on one side of the jaw only. They differ also in name, for wild and fierce ones are called beasts or wild beasts (bestiae, ferae), as Isidore says, while the domestic ones are properly called beasts of burden (iumenta) or herd-animals (pecora). Of domestic animals: some serve for use only, as horses and asses, and these are properly called iumenta, as though iuvamenta, "helpers"; some serve only to be eaten, as sheep, rams and lambs, and these are called pecudes, as though pecuedes; and some serve both for the labour of use and for food, as oxen and the like, and these are properly called pecora - though often one term is used for another. Let us then speak first of the domestic animals, which are of greater use, more for the reader's pleasure than for the student's advancement.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 2] On the ox
div.p: The ox, as Isidore and Ambrose say, is an animal most patient of labour, simple and gentle; whence the Greeks call the ox trion, as though terion, because in ploughing it wears down (terit) the earth - as Naevius says: "here the rustic driver of the plough-oxen." Oxen show such devotion to their yoke-fellows, Ambrose says, that an ox seeks out, circling and lowing, the companion with whom it is used to drawing the plough; and when one of the pair grows weary beneath the yoke, the other, as if in sympathy, lows and pulls the plough all the harder, so that its companion may be spared; and if its accustomed yoke-fellow is changed for another, it despairs at its labour and no longer feels itself as safe or as strong as before.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 2, note] Further on the ox and the bull
div.p: Also, as Ambrose says, when rain is coming the ox keeps close to its stall and is with difficulty made to leave it, but when fair weather is coming it stretches its neck out beyond the stall and, unbidden by anyone, is eager to go out to pasture; this too, from the behaviour of oxen, is a further sign of fair or stormy weather to come, as Virgil says in the Georgics: "be wary of rain" when "the heifer, gazing at the sky, has caught the breeze with wide-open nostrils." Solinus says that in India there are one-horned and three-horned oxen, a very powerful breed having solid, undivided hooves, unlike other oxen. In Egypt, the same author says, there is an ox called Apis, having a white mark on its right flank in the shape of, and the size of, a crescent moon with horns; this kind of ox has a fixed span of life which it does not exceed, but when it has reached the appointed time it plunges into a certain spring and dies. This same ox, however, refuses to take food from anyone's hand if it foretells misfortune; the boys who follow it about, once it has been caught, become as if seized with frenzy and, in their madness, foretell things to come. "A weary ox plants its foot more firmly," as Jerome says in his letter to Augustine, and perhaps all weary animals do the same. The skin of the ox, from the neck to the legs, is called in the plural palearia, "dewlaps"; Virgil in the Georgics: "the dewlaps hang down to the legs." For the signs of a good and strong ox, and how they ought to be fed and pastured, one should consult Virgil's Georgics. Oxen, Isidore says, are properly called armenta, as though armamenta, because in certain regions they are put into military service, as in parts of Italy, where armed men are accustomed to draw wagons drawn by them. A young ox (iuvencus) is so called from iuvare, "to help" - that is, a youthful ox, Isidore says, because it is just beginning to be of help to man's use; or else because among the pagans it was the young ox, never the full-grown bull, that was sacrificed to Jove. "Bull" (taurus) is, like "ox," a Greek word, Isidore says, and the bull is a more stubborn and lustful animal, and less suited to the plough. Whence Ovid: "the bull, led from the herd, balks at the plough." The signs of a good bull are these, which Virgil sets down in the Bucolics, saying: "feed the bull that will already butt with his horn and paw the sand with his feet." Solinus says that in India there are tawny-coloured bulls, far swifter than others, with hair growing backward against the grain; their mouths gape so wide that they consume whatever they seize in them, and, contrary to the nature of all other animals, they can move their horns wherever they wish. Their hide is so tough that they fear no weapon, and they are so fierce and untamable that they will die before they can be tamed.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 3] On the cow
div.p: The cow (vacca), Isidore says, is the female of the ox by a change of one letter, as though bacca were boacca, just as leaena comes from leo and dracaena from draco. She is likewise called vitula, from a young (vivens) ox, and iuvenca, from iuvencus. In all animals, as Aristotle says, the female has a thinner voice than the male, except in the cow alone, which has a deeper voice than the bull. Isidore says that vitula properly denotes a cow that has not yet calved; once she has calved she is either a iuvenca or a vacca. The Observer (Experimentator) says that bees are generated from the putrid flesh of calves exposed to the sun.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 4] On sheep
div.p: The sheep (ovis), Isidore says, is a gentle animal, of comely body and mild temper, and has the softest wool of all animals; sheep are so named from oblatio, "offering," because in ancient times it was not larger animals but sheep alone that were customarily offered in sacrifice. Among sheep, Isidore says, some are called bidentes, "two-toothed," because among their eight teeth two stand higher, which the pagans used to offer in sacrifice. Sheep, as Ambrose says, on the approach of winter eat the grass more eagerly and vigorously, as if wishing to fill themselves well on the green pasture before winter burns it away; and sheep can smell a wolf, and before they even see it coming they gather and huddle together as if for battle - but as soon as it draws near them, they at once scatter and flee. The wether (vervex), Isidore says, is named from vires, "strength," because it is stronger than the other sheep, or because it is, as it were, the head (vertex) of the flock - that is, the male - or else because it has a worm (vermis) in its head at the place where the horns meet the skull, and from the itching this causes they are provoked against one another to butt and fight with their horns. Virgil says in the Bucolics that ewes with lambs eat willow-branches very readily. He likewise says there that sheep, in the morning, eat the dew most eagerly and greedily, whence shepherds in those regions where the dew falls heaviest and sweetest - as in every northern land - are accustomed to drive their sheep out to pasture only after sunrise, once the dew has lifted, because otherwise the sheep would eat so much of it that they would die. The ram (aries) is named from arae, "altars," Isidore says, because the ancients were the first to begin sacrificing rams; whence the line: "and the ram is slain upon the sacred altar."

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 5] On the lamb
div.p: The lamb (agnus), Isidore says, is so named from agnoscere, "to recognize," because more than any other animal it recognizes its mother - so much so, Ambrose says, that among a thousand sheep it seeks out its known mother by her bleat and her scent, and will suck the udder of no one but its own mother; the mother likewise recognizes her own young among the other sheep and offers her udder to no one but her own lamb - whence the mother calls her young by bleating, and the young answers its mother in turn. It is a simple and gentle animal. The wool of lambs is softer, and helps all abscesses when applied in poultices upon them, and because of its sponginess it is effective against swelling. The flesh of young lambs is very phlegmatic, and for this reason is not good to eat when boiled, but is better roasted or stewed, since fire breaks down its rawness and its watery fat.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 6] On the he-goat
div.p: The he-goat (hircus) is a very lustful, wanton and lascivious animal, ever burning for mating, and for this reason always looks sideways - whence also its name, being called hircus as though hirquus, for hirqui, Isidore says, are the corners of the eyes. Of which Virgil says in the Bucolics: "we too have known you, looking askance at the he-goats as they eye you sideways." Its nature is so hot, Isidore says, that its blood, because of the force of its heat, bursts forth against whoever loves it too closely.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 6, note] Uses of the he-goat's blood
div.p: The Observer says that the blood of the he-goat and of the goose, mixed with olive-lees and vinegar, so softens glass and gems placed in it that they can be cut with a blade.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 6, note 2] Further on the he-goat's blood
div.p: The blood of the he-goat, put into must, hastens its clarification; cheese, on the contrary, put into it, hinders it. The blood of the he-goat, as Aristotle says, coagulates very quickly. Its flesh is malodorous and unfit to eat, except for the testicles. In Libya, Solinus says, there are he-goats called Cinyphes, larger and more vigorous than others, named from the river Cinyps, from whose water they draw greater strength than other he-goats.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 7] On the she-goat
div.p: The she-goat (capra) is a somewhat melancholic animal, and is named, according to Isidore, from carpere, "to nibble," because it most greedily nibbles at shrubs, especially in mountainous and rocky places; for this reason its hooves are as it were hollow and sharp at the tips, so that it may keep its footing better on the rocks. Or else goats are named from the crepitus, "clatter," of their legs, because they make a clattering noise as they walk, owing to the hardness and hollowness of their hooves. Goat's flesh is unpleasant and unfit to eat, but goat's milk is excellent and very rich in butter-fat; for it is a general rule that the drier an animal is, the more buttery and better its milk - as with goat's milk and ass's milk - while the fatter the animal, the more watery and poorer its milk.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 7, note] Medicinal uses of goat products
div.p: The Observer says that goat's milk, boiled down with mint, quickly relieves a woman after childbirth. Goat's whey is also very good for those with fever and useful in other remedies. Goat's tallow, applied in ointments, is excellent and helps in cases of nerve weakness and paralysis. The Observer also says that an epileptic fumigated with the smoke of goat's horn will fall down at once. Ambrose says that a wounded goat eats dittany, and that if it has an arrow in its body, the dittany draws it out - though Solinus says this of deer.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 8] On the kid
div.p: The kid (hedus), according to Isidore, is named from edere, "to eat," for its flesh is very tender, good and useful to eat, and of pleasant flavour. It is a general rule that the young of animals with good milk have good flesh while still living, on account of the goodness of the milk on which they feed - and for this reason kid's flesh is good, though goat's flesh is unpleasant. The young of animals with watery milk, however, have worse flesh while living, since they feed on watery milk - and for this reason lamb's flesh is not as good as kid's flesh. Aristotle, in his book On Animals, says that a he-goat was once found that gave milk in such quantity that cheese was made from it, and that this is even possible if the area around the udder and teats is rubbed vigorously and often with the juice of nettle. The urine of the he-goat and she-goat, as Aristotle says, is very thin, on account of the heat of their blood. The he-goat and the ram, when about to butt, step back a good way so as to strike the harder.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 9] On the pig
div.p: The pig is a phlegmatic, filthy and unclean animal; whence porcus is named, according to Isidore, as though spurcus, "filthy." For it delights in mud and mire, and not only eats human excrement but wallows in it. It is also called sus because it roots up (subigit) its pasture - that is, it works the ground to seek its food. Virgil says in the Georgics that when pigs disdain to root up the clods and seek only grass and herbage in the fields, it is a sign of fair weather. Boars are also called verres, because they have great strength (vires). Pork is not wholesome, because it has too much watery fat; for, as Aristotle says in his book On Life and Death, not all fat is of one kind - some is watery and greasy, like pig fat, and some is oily and airy, like the fat of birds. The extremities of pigs, such as the feet and head, are better, because the movement in the extremities dries out the moist phlegmatic humour there. Pigs, as Aristotle says, are killed above all by quinsy, as are dogs. Pigs are fond of one another and show great mutual sympathy: when one pig cries out, the others nearby, as far as they can hear, run up and help the injured one - the contrary happens with dogs, for if one dog bites someone, all the other dogs then set upon the injured party. The bristles of pigs are called setae; whence Virgil: "this head of the bristly boar for you, Delia, a small gift," and so on. Aristotle says that bristly animals have no horns, because the nourishment that would go to horns goes instead to their bristles. The milk of the pig, as Aristotle says, is very watery and provides little nourishment, and the sow has this peculiarity, that she gives her first teat to her first-born. Pigs, as Aristotle says, are fattened in this manner: on the first day water is to be given them to drink, and on the second none; then they are to be fed for three or four days, and after that left alone until the seventh day, after which they should be given barley or millet or oat chaff. Aristotle also says that a sixth part of a pig's food goes to its bristles and the remaining five-sixths to its flesh, and that a pig lives fifteen years and can conceive after three years.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 10] On the wild boar
div.p: The wild boar (aper), Isidore says, is named as though afer, that is, "wild" (ferus), and so it is called aper silvestris, "wild boar," because it is fierce, just as there are both domestic pigs and wild pigs. The wild pig has the same form as the domestic pig, but is larger in body and strength, and has two of its outer teeth more prominent and sharper. The wild boar, as Aristotle says, mates until the age of three years, and what it begets after growing old is poor, ugly and small of body. The young born in winter are also better, Aristotle says, than those born in summer, and the fatter a boar becomes, the more it is able to mate, especially in the morning. The female wild pig conceives after three years and carries in the womb for two years, during which time she is never approached by the boar at all, as Aristotle says, and afterward bears a single large offspring resembling a calf.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 11] On dogs
div.p: The dog (canis), Isidore says, is so named from the sound (canor) of its barking, or from the Greek kynos, "dog." Dogs, as Isidore, Pliny, Solinus, Ambrose and Aristotle all say, are among the most intelligent of animals, possessed of an industrious sense, keenness of smell and swiftness of body, as is shown by the size of their foreheads - for, in proportion to their bodies, they have a broad and very long forehead, which is a sign of industry, as Aristotle says in his Physiognomy. Dogs, more than any other animal, recognize their own names and love their masters while dreading strangers - though hunting dogs belonging to shepherds and country folk are less fearful of strangers. They guard their masters' homes, throw themselves into the face of death for their masters, and will not willingly abandon even their masters' dead bodies; sometimes they hunt to please their masters, driven neither by hunger nor by hatred of the beast they pursue nor by natural enmity toward it. For these reasons dogs lie in wait for other animals more than any other creature does. Solinus relates that a certain dog in Epirus publicly denounced, before the bystanders, the murderer of its master, standing over the corpse of the slain man. Blessed Ambrose says a similar thing happened at Antioch. Solinus says that the kings of the Garamantes led two hundred dogs with them into battle against their enemies. Solinus also says that in Albania there are dogs of such size and strength that they can even overthrow and kill lions and elephants. In India, the same author says, bitches are tied up at night in the woods so that they may conceive by tigers; the first litters of such a mating are weak, but later ones are stronger. Egyptian dogs, the same author says, never drink from the Nile except while running, so as not to be caught by crocodiles. The licisca is a large, strong dog, such as shepherds' dogs are, born of a lynx and a domestic dog; of which Virgil says in the Bucolics: "to catch by ambush, with much barking of the licisca?" There are two kinds of hunting dogs: greyhounds (veltres), which track wild beasts by scent, and harriers (leverarii), which have a weaker sense of smell but are swifter and stronger. A dog, as Ambrose says, when pursuing a beast and coming to a fork in the paths, follows the place as if by syllogism and division, and finds the true branch, reasoning within itself in this way: "either it went by this path or by that one; but not by that one" - this it grasps by scent - "therefore perhaps by this one"; and it examines and searches this in the same way, by the keenness of its scent, until it comes upon the trail. No animal, as Aristotle says, remains locked together in mating except the dog alone, and this because of the constriction of the bitch's womb.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 11, note] Further curiosities of dogs
div.p: The milk of the dog is thicker than that of other animals, as Aristotle says. Solinus says that dogs which happen by any chance to taste menstrual blood are turned to madness. Aristotle: every animal bitten by a mad dog goes mad, except man. The most common ailments among dogs are quinsy, rabies, gout and mange, and few dogs recover from these, above all from rabies and gout. The Observer says that dogs which are fed a frog become mute. Whence in Virgil it is said of the three-headed dog [Cerberus] that a morsel is thrown to it. Puppies (catuli) are properly the young of dogs, Isidore says, though by extension the young of other animals are also called catuli, just as the young of all birds are called pulli.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 12] On horses
div.p: Horses (equi) are so named, Isidore says, because in teams of four they were matched (aequales) in strength and vigour for pulling. The horse is also called caballus from cavare, "to hollow," because it hollows the earth with its hoof; and sonipes, because its feet make a ringing sound (sonitus) as it runs; and cornipes, because it has horny hooves on its feet. It is a strong, spirited and exultant animal. It is roused to battle by the sound of the trumpet, and horses fight among themselves with bites and kicks no less fiercely than their riders fight. Some even recognize their own masters and allow no one else to mount them, nor even to be caught or handled by another. Many of them weep when their masters are slain; for no animal weeps, Aristotle says, except man and the horse. From the sadness or high spirits of horses, Isidore says, many foretell the outcome of a battle, as if from a sure sign. Persian, Epirot and Sicilian horses live longer than others, living up to fifty years, as Solinus says. The best horses are found in Cappadocia; Spanish, Numidian, Gallic and German horses do not live so long. Pliny says that mares are swifter than stallions; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "does Epirus send forth the palms of Elean mares?" Isidore says that the ideal conformation of a horse is: a long flank, round haunches, broad chest, the whole body well-knit, slender and dry legs, hollow hooves, a small and lean head, short and pricked ears, large eyes, wide nostrils, an arched neck, a thick mane and likewise tail, hooves solid, firm and round, a bold spirit, a lively step, and trembling in the other limbs - which in a horse is a sign of strength - and it should be easily roused by the spur and, once roused, easily restrained when desired. The speed of a horse, Isidore says, is judged by its ears: if its ears are mobile, speed is presumed; strength is judged by trembling of the limbs, for if it has trembling limbs, strength is presumed. The principal colours of horses, Isidore says, are these: blue-grey (bladius), golden, rose, myrtle, deer-coloured, dun, grey-blue, dappled, hoary, white, spotted, black, and pied (that is, marked with black and blue-grey), and ash-coloured - fifteen colours of horses in all. According to Isidore, bladius is a colour mixed of rose and black; aureus we may simply call red; roseus has a redness mixed with white; myrteus is said to have more of red in it; cervinus is what the Germans commonly call the colour of murex-purple, or airy; gilvus is a whitish colour; glaucus is as if having painted eyes suffused with a certain brightness; scutulatus is said of one having white spots amid purple colouring; canus is composed of white and black; guttatus is one having black spots distinct amid white, or white amid black; cinereus, also called dosinus, is like the colour of a donkey. The kinds of horses, Isidore says, are three: the first is noble, suited to war and battle; the second is common and used in herds for journeys and labour, and among the ancients this kind was called veredus, from vehere redas, "to draw wagons" - that is, public goods; the third is a hybrid (bigenerum) produced by the crossing of the two kinds, such as the mule. Solinus says that the horse of Alexander the Great, named Bucephalus because it had the head of a bull marked in white upon its shoulder, once it had been fitted with the royal saddle, allowed no one but Alexander to mount it. This horse delivered Alexander from great dangers, and so, when it died, Alexander held funeral rites for it and founded a city in its name, which he called Bucephala. The king of the Cythians, as Solinus says, when he had been struck down in single combat and the victor wished to strip him of his arms, had his horse tear the adversary apart with its teeth. Among horses, Solinus says, the male lives longer than the female, for a horse was found, the same author says, that lived to the age of seventy; and horses, Solinus says, can breed up to the age of thirty-three. Mares, Solinus says, are deprived of their desire to mate if their manes are cut off, since their wantonness is thought to reside in their locks or manes.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 12, note] Further on horses
div.p: Horses, as Aristotle says, recognize their mothers very well, and are so modest that they will knowingly neither mate with nor approach their own mothers. The Observer says that a pregnant mare, if she smells the smoke of an extinguished candle, will miscarry. A horse, as Aristotle says, prefers to drink muddy water rather than clear; hence, when it comes to clear water, it stirs it up with its hoof. A cow, however, always prefers clear water.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 13] On mules
div.p: The mule is generated, contrary to nature, from a donkey and a mare, just as the hinny (burdo) is generated from a stallion and a she-ass; but the breed of hinnies is uglier, weaker and less fit for use. The mule, however, is a strong animal, able to bear great burdens and endure much labour, though it does not run swiftly. It mates excessively and at any time of year, whereas other animals have fixed seasons for mating; and for this reason it is said: "be not like the horse and the mule." Isidore says that a certain Anah, a grandson of Esau, was the first to discover the art of breeding mules, for he had donkeys mount mares in the wilderness, so that strong asses might be born from this union. Mules are sterile, and the cause of this is, according to some, that a mule is difficult to breed from its parents [i.e. is itself a hybrid of two different species], and so its seed is, so to speak, interpreted according to its distance from the temperament of its parents; and thus the generative power, having already been weak and difficult in its begetters, fails altogether in what is begotten by it. Aristotle, however, says that the cause of their sterility is that female mules do not retain the seed but expel it, and he says that if they retained it, they would breed, just as other animals do.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 14] On the donkey
div.p: The donkey (asinus), according to Isidore, is named from sedendo, "sitting," or from sella, "saddle," or according to others from a, "without," and senos, "sense." It is altogether a simple animal, refusing no burden however heavy. It is very slow, but has a very strong and load-bearing back. It knows nothing of discord or malice, but is simple and most gentle: when it senses a wolf approaching from afar it prepares itself as if to defend itself, but once the wolf draws near it flees and hides its head among the bushes, believing itself entirely hidden simply because it can no longer see. When a herd of donkeys travels along a narrow path where they cannot turn aside, if the one in front should stumble or hurt its foot, the one behind, even if beaten, will refuse to go on, as if avoiding the same danger.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 14, note] On donkey's milk and hide
div.p: Donkey's milk is, of all milks, the whitest both in itself and in its effect; hence we read that Nero's wife often bathed in donkey's milk. Its bones, too, resemble ivory, but, unlike ivory, do not redden with age. The Observer says that whoever sleeps on a donkey's hide is safe from demons and phantoms. A ring made from the right hoof of a donkey helps an epileptic if he wears it. A belt of donkey hide does the same for a woman troubled by an incubus.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 15] On the wild ass
div.p: The wild ass (onager), Isidore says, is a very wild and savage donkey, and is named from the Greek onos, "ass," and agrios, "wild." These, Solinus says, are found in the deserts of Africa, and are large and untamable animals. They divide their herds by females, Isidore says, and a single male presides over each herd. When the females give birth, the males follow them and try to attack the male young, to bite off their testicles and prevent them from one day succeeding to leadership of the herd of females - but the mothers hide them. In Arcadia there are large domestic donkeys resembling wild asses, Isidore says, and for this reason large donkeys are called Arcadian, from the place whence they were first brought. Wild asses have a fixed time for all their activities, above all for mating, whence it is said in the Prophet: "the wild ass in the desert knows its season." They are wild and untamable, as Aristotle says, because they can endure thirst for a long time, until the rivers are free of the approach of all other beasts. The Psalm says: "the wild asses shall wait in their thirst," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 16] On the camel
div.p: The camel, Isidore says, is named from the Greek word cami, meaning "low" or "bent," because when camels are to be loaded, their driver gives a signal in public with a whip, so that the camel bends and stoops to receive its burden. It is a large animal of extraordinary height and stature, its back curved in the middle, with long legs and cloven feet, a rather short tail and a small head, but a slender neck, so that it is not burdensome to it - for it is very long, as Ambrose says, precisely so that it can reach the ground, since it takes its food, grasses and herbs, from there. Camels are numerous in Arabia, though they are also found in other lands; merchants there use them to carry goods. Arabian camels, Isidore says, differ from others in this: that camels of other regions have only one hump on their back, but Arabian camels have two humps on their back, and there is also another kind of camel used not for burdens but for travel. Both kinds share this trait, Solinus says, that the burden-bearers take on no more of a load than they can carry, and the travel-camels likewise run no more than their accustomed distance in a day. Bactrian camels, Solinus says, never wear down their feet. The whole camel kind is impatient of excess and grows fierce at mating time. Camels feel great hatred toward horses, and can endure thirst for four days; they willingly drink muddy water, as Aristotle says, and once they have had the chance to drink their fill, they drink so much that they will be content even without drinking again for some time to come. When the water is clear, a camel stirs it up with its foot before drinking. They live a hundred years in their natural and accustomed habitats. Female camels, Solinus says, are also raised for war and are castrated, so that, deprived of mating, they become stronger.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 17] On the camelopard
div.p: Solinus reports that in Ethiopia there is an animal called by the natives nabus, but among us called the camelopard; it has a neck like a horse's, feet like a buffalo's, and the head of a camel, and over its whole body it has bright, gleaming white spots on an otherwise whitish coat.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 18] On the dromedary
div.p: The dromedary, Isidore says, is an animal of the camel kind, but smaller in body and stature, and much swifter in running, most suited for travel; it can cover a hundred miles or more in a single day. This animal chews the cud, like the ox, the sheep and the camel. Rumination (ruminatio) is named from the rumen, a certain protruding part of the throat, in which ruminant animals store their food before bringing it back up to the mouth to chew a second time. The dromedary is named from the Greek dromos, "course" or "running." The rider or driver of a dromedary is called a dromedarius. Whence the verse: "Dromos means a course, and from this we call the dromedary; and I call their riders, by the same root, dromedarii."

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 19] On the buffalo
div.p: The buffalo (bubalus), as Aristotle and Isidore say, is a wild ox; the finest breed of these oxen, Solinus says, is found in Africa, and they are like domestic oxen in their whole body except that they are larger, and so wild and untamable that they will not accept the yoke on their necks - so that the buffalo is, despite the diminutive form of its name, in fact a large ox. Sea-oxen (marine buffalo?), Pliny says, have beards on their chin, long in place of dewlaps, and above their shoulders, at the end of the neck, a great forked hump shaped like a saddle.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 20] On the aurochs
div.p: Aurochs (uri), as Isidore and Solinus say, are large, untamable wild oxen born only in the forests of Germany, which some call buffalo, though they are not buffalo. These, Solinus says, have bull-like horns of such length and spread that from them are made drinking vessels so splendid that their use is fitting at royal tables, for they are black and take a natural polish that gives them a certain sheen, and they hold a great volume owing to their size. They are caught in the German forests with dogs and by hunting.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 21] On the fallow deer
div.p: The fallow deer (dama), or by diminutive damula, is so named, Isidore says, because it escapes (effugiat) from the hand (de manu) of its captor - whence dama as though "from the hand." It is a timid and unwarlike animal, having no means of defence at all. Whence the verse of Martial: "the boar defends itself with its tusk, horns defend the stag; are we unwarlike deer nothing but prey?" More than any other animal, they fear dogs above all. Whence Virgil in the Bucolics says, as an image of the impossible: "and the timid deer shall come to drink alongside the following hounds."

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 22] On the hare
div.p: The hare (lepus), Isidore says, is likewise a timid and unwarlike animal, but excels greatly in speed and flight; whence lepus is named as though levipes, "light-foot." It does not so much escape dogs by outright flight and speed as by doubling back; for it does not flee in a straight line but in zigzags. Hares are especially fond of green barley, and sleep with their eyes open. They have only two [front] teeth. Their front feet are shorter, their hind feet longer; hence they run faster uphill than downhill. When a hare has had abundant food, Ambrose says, it changes its coat in winter and returns to its former colour afterward in summer; hence many hares are caught by their white coats - not, as some think, because of old age, but because of abundance of food. Some say that hares have an indeterminate sex, but this is not true; according to Aristotle, every blooded animal has a distinct sex, one being male, the other female. The hare, in proportion to its body, has a large heart, because it is a timid animal - for Aristotle says that animals with large hearts are timid, and those with small hearts are bold; whence the lion has, relative to its body, a very small heart.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 23] On the squirrel
div.p: The squirrel (spariolus) is so named from spargere, "to scatter," because it scatters about the nuts and fruits on which it feeds until it chooses the best of them; it is a small animal, with a solid, strong head and keen sight. It has a large, bushy tail, with fine hairs like feathers, by means of which it flies from tree to tree and shelters itself from rain, laying its tail over its body from back to head. As they grow old, their fur begins to redden somewhat. When they cannot find sufficient and good pasture, they run in troops through many provinces and regions, from forest to forest, appointing two guards, one in front and one behind. They swim across rivers by the effort of their feet and the sail of their tail. They have two very sharp teeth for gnawing through nutshells, and they utter a very loud, rather frightening cry. Some make their nests low in trees, near the roots; others in burrows and hollows in the ground.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 24] On otters
div.p: Otters (caniculi), according to Isidore, are so named because they are caught and driven from their dens by the tracking of dogs (canes), or else they are named from cuniculi, "burrows," for they have burrows - that is, hidden holes - along the banks of waters, and they move both on land and in water, though in water only with intermittent breathing. They feed chiefly on fish, which they hunt along the shores. Platearius says: the caniculus (otter) is so named from its hunting of fish, or from cuniculi, the burrows or holes in the riverbanks where it lives, or lutra from lutum, "mud," in which it hides itself from dogs.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 25] On the badger
div.p: The badger (melus or taxus) is so named, according to Isidore, because its genital member is perfectly round - for melin in Greek means "round" in Latin - or else because it seeks out and greatly desires honeycombs. This animal is also given to raiding vineyards, and is often caught there. It is a creature of great cunning: it lays up various kinds of food for itself against the winter, and for this reason the fox, itself a cunning animal, watches for the badger's den and, while the badger is away, deposits its own dung inside it. When the badger returns and finds its den thus fouled, unable to bear the stench, it abandons the den, and the fox then enjoys everything the badger had gathered there. The badger has a head like a pig's, a thick, fat body, feet and claws like a bear's, a short tail, and what appear to be two openings at its rear, though in fact there is only one anal opening.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 26] On the fox
div.p: The fox (vulpes), Isidore says, is named as though volupes, "rolling-foot," for it does not run straight but in twists and turns when fleeing dogs. It is a most cunning animal, ever bent on deceiving and laying snares for other animals. Isidore says the fox has this trick: when hungry, it lies down in furrows and public roads and feigns death, and when birds fly down to it, it seizes and devours them. Aristotle says the lion shares its prey, and the fox, knowing this, follows it to feed on the remains of the lion's kill; yet it gains no real advantage from this trickery, for if the lion's catch does not suffice, it seizes and devours the fox that has been following it. Ambrose says that when the fox falls sick it eats the resin flowing from pine trees, and is cured by this. He also says that, among all animals, foxes take the greatest care for their young, in whom they place, as it were, their hope of posterity - and this is because of abundance of food, for the fox always provides abundantly for itself and its young, and for this reason it often changes its dens too, fearing betrayal. The Observer says that when foxes are domesticated they steal everything.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 27] On the beaver
div.p: Beavers (castores), Isidore says, are named from castrando, "castrating."
