It is a strange-looking animal, four-footed in its front part but with feet like a goose behind, and ending in a fish's tail. This animal's testicles are used in medicine and are called castoreum; and the animal, knowing that it is above all pursued for this reason, as soon as it is set upon, bites off its own testicles. Hence beavers are named from castrating, of which Juvenal says: "he who makes himself a eunuch, wishing to escape the loss of his testicle." Whence another writes: "let the question be resolved, when the beaver is put to flight by its enemy, why it bears in the ablative what it once bore in the genitive [i.e. loses what it once possessed]." Yet this has rarely or never actually been observed by those experienced in hunting them; moreover, the testicles called castoreum lie so deep within the animal's body that it could never remove them without risking its own life. Solinus says the beaver has such sharp teeth that if it seizes a man or dog in its jaws, it does not release its grip until it feels its teeth meet through the flesh or bone. This animal builds itself nests of wood near water, but lives in hidden burrows along the water's edge, and where it must cross water it builds itself a bridge of wood; with the sharpness of its teeth it fells great trees, and it knows very well how to guard itself from harm as they fall. This animal is also called by another name, fiber; many, and very large ones, Solinus says, are born around the Black Sea (Pontus).

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 28] On the ibex
div.p: Ibexes (ybices), Isidore says, are so named as though abices, because, like birds, they keep to the heights of mountains and crags. They are also called capreae, "wild goats." While alive they have very hollow and extremely sharp hooves, so that they may better keep their footing on rocks and precipices. They have very keen sight, so that on seeing a man or a beast from afar, they immediately hurl themselves down and land unharmed upon their horns. They always bear twins, and at once teach them to walk and to leap over precipices; one twin stays hidden while the other is trained with the mother among the cliffs.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 29] On the stag
div.p: The stag (cervus), Isidore says, is named from the Greek keraton, meaning "horns" in Latin, for it is an animal especially armed and distinguished by its horns. Stags, Solinus says, become very fierce and bold at mating season, and do not conceive before the rising of the star Arcturus. They raise their young not in one place but in several, so as to hide them better, setting them among thickets; and when the fawns wish to go out, the mother strikes them with her hoof and forces them to remain among the bushes. Once they are grown, she rouses them to go out and, by encouragement, teaches them to leap over rough ground. When dogs pursue them, stags run, if they can, with the wind at their backs, so that their scent may fall away behind them - though the opposite is often seen, since they flee above all toward water. They are greatly startled by the sound of pipes and hear it very acutely, when they prick up their ears; but with their ears lowered they hear nothing. They are easily frightened and are much afraid when swimming across water. They find their paths and fords more by scent than by sight. In each herd, the sick stags are placed at the rear, and the others take turns tending them, supporting them with their horns and haunches.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 29, notes] Medicinal and other properties of the stag
div.p: The right horn of the stag, Solinus says, is more useful in medicine, for driving away serpents; burnt stag's horn is also very effective, for serpents flee the smell of its smoke. The same fumigation also changes the smell of wine and reveals epilepsy. A stag's horns grow until it is six years old; after that they will not visibly increase in number of points, though they may grow somewhat larger still. A castrated stag's horns neither grow nor, if it already has them, fall off. Its teeth reveal its age, whether young or old. When sick, a stag goes and, by the breath of its nostrils, draws serpents out of their lairs, swallows them, and by this is purged and healed. It eats the herb dittany when wounded by a weapon, and by eating it, expels the arrow from the wound. It also eats the herb called cynaris as a remedy against harmful grasses and herbs. The rennet of a fawn killed while still in its mother's womb is, Solinus says, a most effective remedy against poison and venom. Stags never suffer fever, and for this reason ointments made from their marrow or fat relieve the heat of feverish patients; whoever eats stag's flesh fasting in the morning will never suffer fevers, as Solinus says. Solinus relates that Alexander the Great placed collars around the necks of certain stags and released them, which, caught again a hundred years later, still appeared young - for they are exceedingly long-lived. Whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "and the branching horns of Mycon's long-lived stag," and so on. Aristotle says that the stag alone, among all animals, has solid horns, for all other animals have hollow ones. He also says that in the stag's heart is found a small bone, highly medicinal against fevers when powdered and taken in wine by a fasting patient.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 30] On the tragelaph (goat-stag)
div.p: The tragelaphus, Isidore says, is Greek for what in Latin is called hircocervus, "goat-stag." It has the whole body of a stag, but has shaggy shoulders and a long chin with a shaggy, long beard like a he-goat's, for which reason it bears the compound name hircocervus, being made up, like its body, of goat and stag. Solinus calls these "striped stags," and says they are found nowhere but around the river Phasis; hence Aristotle too, as though it were an unknown and imaginary creature, often uses it as an example in his books.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 31] On the lion
div.p: The lion, Isidore holds, is named from the Greek leon, which we call in Latin leo, and it is interpreted as "king," because it is the prince of all beasts. There are three kinds of lions, Isidore says: the Numidian, found in Africa, which are short, have curly manes, and are unwarlike, not as spirited as the Indian lions - whence Solinus says that Numidian lions fear the Indian ones and, as it were, blush at their own smallness compared to them. The Arabian lions, after these, are spirited and strong. A sign of spiritedness in them is a broad, open forehead, a wide and expansive chest, and a mobile, long tail. Their strength lies in the chest, firmness in the head and jaws; the hindquarters of their body are weaker. When surrounded by hunters, they fix their gaze on the ground, so as not to be frightened by the sight of the spears. They fear the creaking of wheels, but above all fear fire, and also the cock, especially a white one. The lion sleeps with its eyes open. When fleeing from a hunt, it wipes away its tracks with its tail so as not to be traced by the hunters. When a lioness has given birth to a cub or cubs, they do not yet come to life for three days and nights; on the third day the father comes and shakes the whole den with his roar, and so, at the sound of his roaring, his offspring seem to awaken and come to life. When a lion roars, all animals are afraid; whence in the Prophet: "the lion shall roar; who shall not fear?" The lion is not angered at man unless it is hungry or provoked. It has a noble spirit even in its fury and vengeance, for it spares those it has laid low and does not harm them further; whence Ovid: "the greater one is, the more readily one's anger is appeased, and a generous mind is easily moved; it is enough for the magnanimous lion to have laid its enemy low - the fight ends once the foe lies prostrate; but the wolf, and the ignoble bear, and every beast of lesser nobility, press on against the dying." The lion's especial mercy, Isidore says, is shown toward fleeing captives, whom, when it sees them, it does not touch as they pass but allows to escape freely. As Aristotle and Solinus say, the lion alone, among animals with many toes on their feet, is born already able to see - though this is said only of African lions, lest it contradict what Isidore says, that newborn lion cubs sleep for three days. Also, a lion drinks on one day and eats on the next, Solinus says; and when it has not digested well, it forgoes food taken the following day and does not eat again until it has digested the previous meal, and when it has eaten too much and feels weighed down, it presses its claws to its mouth and tries to draw out the excess flesh it has taken. Lions spare above all women and children among humankind. They mate turned away from one another, and in their first litter bear five cubs, Solinus says; thereafter each year the number decreases by one, until the lioness finally becomes barren. When pursued in open plains by dogs and hunters, they turn aside from the path and stand, feigning to have no fear, as if preparing to fight; but in forests they always flee, and their speed in fleeing lies not in running but in leaping. They keep their claws sheathed and drawn into the flesh of their paws, so that they are not blunted by excessive wear and use. They like to dwell in secret and are reluctant to be seen by men or other wild creatures. They are very generous, and share their prey with the animals that follow them. The lion, Ambrose says, when it falls sick, seeks out an ape and devours it raw, and is cured, as if by a kind of medicine, by eating it. He also says that a lion never returns to the remains of its own kill, but always seeks fresh prey whenever it is hungry.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 32] On the leopard
div.p: The leopard, as Pliny says in his Natural History, is born of a lioness and a male pard, or of a female pard and a lion - a hybrid animal, like the mule from a mare and a donkey. This kind, Solinus says, is not as noble or as strong as the lion, being inferior in body and strength, and lacks a mane on the neck. What lion and leopard have in common is that both give birth from an excess of fat. The leopard, Ambrose says, when sick drinks the blood of the ibex, that is, of the wild goat, and is cured by this. The leopard also, the same author says, sometimes abhors the smell of garlic and cannot bear it, but flees from it at once.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 33] On the panther
div.p: The panther, Isidore says, is named because it is a friend to all animals except the dragon, which it greatly hates - or because it not only delights in the company of its own kind, but returns whatever kindness it receives in like measure. Pan in Greek means "all" or "every," theros meaning "beast"; hence panther, as it were, "friend of all." This beast, Isidore says, is of varied colour, its whole hide suffused with black and white intermixed, with tawny circles above like eyes. It bears young only once, for it has very sharp claws, and its own offspring, in the womb, injure the womb with the sharpness of their claws and tear it so badly that she can no longer conceive thereafter - which is what Pliny means in his Natural History when he says that animals with sharp claws cannot often bear young. Solinus relates that flocks of sheep and herds of cattle so admire the panther's scent and appearance, on account of its beautiful markings, that, astonished and with ears pricked, they follow it, gazing, and are not frightened - except by the crookedness of its mouth, for it has a somewhat curved mouth, and for this reason the panther hides its mouth from them, and when the moment is right, leaps into the herd and seizes and devours whatever it wishes. Panthers are born in Hyrcania, and the men there, Solinus says, in order to kill them, sprinkle powder of aconite or hellebore on meat and lay it along the forest paths. But the panther, having eaten this meat and, on feeling the effect of the poison, eats human excrement to cure itself, and so escapes. This animal is so hard to kill that even with its bowels spilled out it can still live a long while.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 34] On the pard
div.p: The pard (pardus), spoken of above as mating with the lioness to produce the leopard: the leopard resembles the panther in the variety of its hide, so much so that in Solinus it is called, as it were, a kind of panther, and it is the swiftest animal after the tiger, and greatly given to bloodshed. It is so swift, Isidore says, that in its leaping it sometimes even hurls itself to its own death. Ambrose says that the pard's varied markings signify not only the mobility of its body but also the inconstancy of its temper; whence the Prophet: "can the leopard change its spots?" and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 35] On the tiger
div.p: The tiger, according to Isidore, is named for its speed, being a most swift and fierce animal - whence the river Tigris too was named after this animal, being the swiftest of all rivers, for the Persians call anything swift "tigris." This animal, Solinus says, is born in Hyrcania and is entirely tawny, with black spots like scattered stars. It is so swift that nothing can escape it, even from a distance; whence, whatever it fails to catch within three leaps, it abandons, as though ashamed and indignant at its own slowness in that instance. Tigers are swiftest of all when roused by the loss of their young. Hunters who steal their cubs make sure the sea is nearby with ships ready, so that as soon as they have snatched the cubs they can board at once - otherwise their attempt is in vain, for they cannot outrun the tiger's speed. When those who have stolen the cubs later return by sea, the tigers recognize them and rush furiously to the shore, and of the many cubs stolen scarcely one can be carried off successfully. Ambrose says that when hunters steal one of her cubs, the mother immediately gives chase; the hunter, mounted on horseback with the cub, flees, carrying with him a large round mirror, which he throws down in the middle of the path behind him; when the pursuing tigress arrives, she sees her own reflection in the mirror and, believing it to be her offspring, sits down beside the mirror on the ground and offers it her teats - and meanwhile the hunter escapes with the cub.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 36] On the rhinoceros
div.p: The rhinoceros, according to Isidore, is named from the Greek rhinos, "nose," and keras, "horn," because it has a single horn on its nose; or it is called monoceros, "one-horned," because it has only one horn, in the middle of its head, rooted as if into the four feet of the head itself, so sharp and strong that whatever it strikes, however hard, it shatters or pierces at the very first blow. It is a fierce and very powerful animal, so much so that it can even overthrow elephants with the thrust of its horn. And it is of such ferocity that it cannot be captured by any hunting method. But, as Isidore and Gregory write in his commentary on Job, a virgin girl is placed in the forest, and the approaching rhinoceros lays its head in her lap and falls asleep there, and thereupon lays aside all its ferocity, so that it may be captured as though unarmed. Solinus says this animal has on its nose a single upward-curving horn, with which it fights the elephant, striking it beneath, in the belly, since in every other part of its body it is not easily wounded. It is similar to a bear in length and shape of body, but greater in strength, and has shorter legs.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 37] On the elephant
div.p: The elephant, Isidore says, is named from the Greek elephyon, "mountain," because in the size of its body it seems equal to a mountain. Among the Indians it is called barrus, from its cry, for "to trumpet" (barrire) is proper to the elephant, as "to roar" is to the lion. Its tusks, Isidore says, are ivory, not ordinary bone as some suppose. In its snout it has a kind of trunk resembling a serpent, with which it takes food from the ground, since it cannot lower its whole head all the way down; and this trunk is protected by a ring of teeth around it. It is an animal that tames quickly, and the Indians use elephants themselves in battle, for they place wooden towers upon them and, armed, fight from those towers, shooting arrows down at the enemy. Elephants have a certain intelligence and, above all, memory greater than other animals; at the sight of blood they take courage for battle - whence it is said in the book of Maccabees: "they showed the elephants the blood of grapes and mulberries, to rouse them for battle," and so on. They travel in herds and greet men with a certain gesture. They mate turned away from one another; they are very afraid of mice and abhor the smell of mice. They are hostile to dragons, and so, when giving birth, hide their young in water or on islands, away from dragons. They carry their young in the womb for two years, and bear only once, and only a single calf, and they live three hundred years. They were once born, Isidore says, in both India and Africa; now, however, only in India. Solinus says elephants observe, by a kind of instinct, the rising and setting of the stars, for by moonlight they go in herds to water and bathe there, and on seeing the sunrise they return at once to the forests, as if paying homage to the star. Their age is marked by the whiteness of their tusks. An elephant always keeps one tusk in use and spares the other, so as to have it stronger for the hour of battle. When they sense they are being hunted, they blunt both tusks through use, wearing them down, because they believe they are pursued chiefly for their ivory. When they travel in herds, the oldest leads the column, and the one behind him follows, guiding the rest of the herd. When they cross a river, the smaller ones go first, so that the heavier and larger ones, by treading the ford, do not make it deeper still. Female elephants do not mate before the age of ten, males not before the age of five. They mate over a two-year period and for no more than five days at a time, and once they have mated they do not return to the herd until they have first bathed. The males never fight over the females. If they see a man wandering lost in the forest, they show him the way to known paths, and do the same for stray herds of cattle. If one of them is wounded, the others gather around it and tend to it. Mauritanian elephants fear the Indian ones, being smaller than they. They are most impatient of cold.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 37, note] Further on the elephant and the dragon
div.p: When an elephant has eaten something poisonous, it seeks out the wild olive and cures itself by eating it. Its back is extremely tough, and it is bristly and shaggy all over except on the belly. When dragons lie in wait for elephants, they position themselves along the paths where they know the elephants will pass, and when the herd goes by they attack the ones at the rear, whom those in front cannot come to aid, since they cannot turn themselves around because of their great size. The dragon wraps its tail around the elephant's legs and bites it in the belly; the elephant, collapsing, kills both itself and the dragon together, and the blood flowing from both beasts, wherever it touches the ground, produces that substance commonly called dragon's blood, which is used in dyes and medicines and also strongly binds the bowels. The cause of the enmity between the dragon and the elephant, Solinus says, is that the dragon is of a very hot nature and burns excessively, while the elephant's blood is very cold, and so the dragon seeks to temper its own heat with the coolness of the elephant's blood. Elephants, however, are tamed more quickly than other animals, especially by drinking barley-water, Solinus says. Ambrose says the elephant has rigid legs without joints or knee-bends, so that its great bulk may be more firmly supported, though its heel bends slightly for the motion of walking. They sleep leaning against very large trees, and so, when hunters wish to capture them, they secretly saw through such trees; when the elephant leans against the tree, it falls together with it and, having no joints, cannot get up again. It lives long, Ambrose says, because all its members are proportioned to its great size.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 38] On the chameleon
div.p: The chameleon is so named, Isidore says, because it very readily takes on every colour it sees, its body changing according to the different colours it beholds. It takes on every colour of whatever it sees, Solinus says, except red and white. It is, Solinus says, a four-footed animal with a face like a lizard's, but with longer legs joined to its belly, a long, mobile, curved tail, and hooked, sharp claws; it moves slowly like a tortoise and has rough, scaly skin like a crocodile's, grim, deep-set eyes, and when it moves the corners of its mouth, its sight sharpens. Its mouth always gapes open, and it takes neither drink nor any other food, but is sustained by breathing air alone. Its body is without flesh and its insides are without intestines, but it has a small heart containing very little blood. In winter it hides, in spring it appears, and it is found nearly throughout all of Asia. The stork eats this creature and swallows it, and dies as soon as it has eaten it. Of this animal there is the verse: "the earth nourishes the mole, the chameleon lives on air; the herring is nourished by the wave, flames feed the salamander." If one objects, citing Aristotle's second book On Generation and Corruption, that nothing simple can nourish, it must be answered that these elements we perceive are not truly simple but have something of the others mixed in, and are named after whichever simple substance predominates in each of them.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 39] On the camelopard
div.p: The camelopard, Isidore says, is an animal resembling the pard, dappled and sprinkled with white spots, but with a neck like a horse's, and feet like a buffalo's. Only in its head does it resemble a camel. It is born only in Ethiopia.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 40] On the lynx
div.p: The lynx, Isidore says, is named from "wolf," being reckoned among the wolf kind. It is a beast marked with various spots, like the pard, but resembling a wolf in stature, its face alone being like a lion's. It also draws in and extends its claws into its flesh, as the lion does. This animal's urine turns into a precious stone, and lynxes themselves, Solinus says, seem in some way aware of this, for as soon as they have urinated they cover it with sand and earth so that the stone will not be found by men. It is called ligurius. Pliny says this animal bears young only once. It is a very strong animal, having a very flexible back and all its limbs swift and agile. Solinus says that this same stone, ligurius, has a colour like amber, attracts threads and chaff, cures kidney pain, and is also effective against jaundice.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 41] On the wolf
div.p: The wolf, according to Isidore, is named from the Greek lykos, which sounds like "wolf" in Latin, and is so called among the Greeks from its bite, since it is an animal always bent on ravening and plunder; or else it is named as though leopos, because, like the lion, its greatest power lies in its feet, since whatever it seizes with them it kills at once. Solinus says that in Italy especially the wolf has this nature: that if the wolf sees a man first, the man is struck dumb, but if the man sees the wolf first, the wolf loses its voice. And for this reason it is said, as a proverb, when someone suddenly enters while being spoken of: "look, the wolf in the story" - since those speaking fall silent at his entrance, as if the man had been struck first by the wolf's gaze. Whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "even Moeris's voice fails him: wolves have seen Moeris first." Solinus says the wolf's tail contains a small tuft of hair of great power as an aphrodisiac, but it has this power and effect only if plucked from the living wolf. Wolves, the same author says, mate only twelve days out of the whole year. They can endure hunger for many days, and if they find no prey, they eat earth. When they are about to attack some large beast, they fill themselves with sand beforehand, so as to be heavier when dragging the prey to the ground, matching their weight to their strength. When a wolf has found prey and is set upon it, if by chance other prey should present itself meanwhile, it at once abandons the first and pursues the new one - such is its greed. They mate, as said, no more than twelve days a year. In Ethiopia, Solinus says, there is a kind of wolf called in Greek the lycaon, which has a mane on its neck and is so varied in colour that no colour is missing from it.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 42] On the cat
div.p: The cat (musio or catus) has two names: musio, because it preys keenly on mice (mures), as Isidore says, or catus, a Greek word meaning "cunning," because it is cunning in its stalking of mice and other small creatures in war against them. One kind of these is wild, another domestic. The Observer says that every cat becomes domestic if its ears are clipped, for after that, once it has felt rain and wind, it grows tame at once.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 43] On the ape
div.p: The ape (symia), Isidore says, is a Greek word with two possible meanings: it may be called simum, "having a flattened nose," in the way that we call men "snub-nosed" - a term Aristotle often uses in his examples - and by this same standard even goats are called symiae, since they too have flattened noses. In another sense it is called symia from similitude, because it appears to resemble a man in the shape of its limbs. The animal is named for both reasons together. This animal's nature, Isidore says, is that apes rejoice at the new and full moon, but grow sad when the moon is waning and dark. When they give birth, they favour some of their young over others, and carry the favoured ones before them, while the rest cling to the mother by themselves. According to Isidore there are five kinds of apes. The first is properly called symia, and these have buttocks but no tails, and come closest to the human form and intelligence. The second, according to Solinus, is called the sphinx, which has bristly, shaggy fur and prominent breasts, and is very docile and quickly tamed. The third kind is called the cynocephali, with dog's heads but the rest of the body like a man's, of whom mention was made above in the treatise on monsters - but whether such monsters can be placed among various species, or fixed in a single one, or whether they constitute a species of their own, is left undetermined for now. The fourth kind are the satyrs, similarly formed and restless with theatrical gestures; these are held in higher regard and put to more use, imitating with great effort every act they see, though they breed only in warm lands. All of them taste and smell any food offered to them before eating it. The fifth kind are called callitriches, quite unlike the others in almost their whole appearance, having a long beard and a broad tail, features found in none of the other kinds. Solinus says apes are caught in this way: the hunter approaches and pretends to anoint his eyes with eel-glue, then withdraws, leaving the glue there; the ape then approaches, wishing to imitate the hunter, and smears its own eyes with the glue, whereupon it can no longer see, and the hunter then comes back and, taking care as he knows how, seizes it.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 44] On the leontophonos
div.p: The leontophonos ("lion-killer"), Isidore says, is a certain small beast, so named for this reason: its flesh, burnt and powdered and scattered upon meat left along a path, kills lions. For this reason, Solinus says, wherever lions find this little creature, they kill it with blows of their paws, but altogether refrain from biting it. This animal is found in Ethiopia, Solinus says.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 45] On the bear
div.p: The bear, Isidore says, is named from urgendo, "pressing" or "forcing," because the young of this animal come forth from the womb only with difficulty, being born too soon - or else because its offspring is shaped by its mouth. For Pliny says that the she-bear gives birth only to a shapeless piece of flesh, which she afterward, with mouth and tongue, works into proper form and features. Whence the saying: "thus the tongue shapes the offspring the bear has brought forth." The cause of this is that she gives birth too quickly, on the thirtieth day, and so the offspring must needs be shapeless. The bear has a weak head, Isidore says, but is very strong in its forelegs, chest and loins, and for this reason always fights standing upright on its hind legs. Ambrose says that when a bear falls sick it eats ants and is cured. Bears, Solinus says, greatly crave honey, and for this reason always lie in wait around beehives. If they happen to taste mandrake apples, they die; and for this reason, Ambrose says, they seek out anthills, since, having been harmed by eating mandrake, they eat ants and are cured. When they attack bulls, they attack first by the horns and the nostrils, for by the horns they can more easily drag them down, and the nostrils too are among the tenderer parts, where they are more easily injured. Bears also, the same Ambrose says, mate face to face, as man does, not turned away as other animals do, and they show great modesty about the act of love. They burden and guard their pregnant females, and mate more readily in winter. When a female bear is pregnant, the male does not approach her, and she makes for herself a separate, special lodging within the same den. While the she-bear is shaping her young, she eats nothing meanwhile, and once she has shaped it she lies hidden, as if asleep, for fourteen days, and thereafter remains still in her den, in darkness, for four months, so that she seems almost blind to herself once she at last comes out into the light.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 46] On the porcupine
div.p: The porcupine (hystrix), Isidore says, is a certain animal in Africa resembling the hedgehog, and is so named because it has long, thick, very sharp quills which, when it moves, rattle as if striking against one another. When it is attacked, or when dogs pursue it in hunting, it releases loosened quills from its back and, like arrows, wounds the pursuing dogs or men.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 47] On the enhydris (otter/ichneumon)
div.p: The enhydris, Isidore says, is a small creature so named because it lives readily and often in water - for hydor in Greek means "water." This animal is found above all in the Nile, and it preys on the crocodile: if it finds one asleep, it first rolls itself in mud, so as to slip in more easily, and enters through the crocodile's mouth, and there tears out and devours all its inner organs, then emerges unharmed, leaving the crocodile dead.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 48] On the suillus (sea-pig / porcupine-fish?)
div.p: The suillus, Isidore says, is a certain animal so named because it is exceedingly fat. Its scent reveals whether food is wholesome or poisoned; whence Dracontius: "the suillus overcomes the force of any poison." It is an animal covered with many bristles, and preys upon the serpent and the asp: when it fights the asp, it raises its tail, and the asp watches this closely as if it were a weapon of war; and when the asp strikes at the tail, the suillus at once coils itself up and kills the asp with the sharpness of its bristles. This is the sea-pig.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 49] On the ferret
div.p: The ferret (furo), Isidore says, is a small animal named from furari, "to steal." It digs dark, hidden burrows and drives out whatever prey it finds within them.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 50] On mice
div.p: The mouse (mus), Isidore says, is named from humor, "moisture," because it is thought to arise from the moisture of the earth - or the word is wholly Greek. This animal's nature, Isidore says, is that its liver grows at the full moon, just as many sea creatures grow at the full moon, such as snails and shellfish. This creature eats only the cleanest things, and yet is itself unclean; the reason, Aristotle says, is that nothing of the food an animal eats passes into its members except what the members themselves draw to them - and like draws to like - so that of the cleanest things it eats, the mouse draws to itself only the coarser and baser parts, and even what good it draws remains undigested. A mouse, when it drinks water, dies, because it is an excessively moist creature.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 50, notes] Further on mice
div.p: The Observer says that hemlock powder mixed with breadcrumbs and scattered about a house kills any mice that eat of it. Of mice, some are wild, some domestic; among these the shrew (sorix) is a kind of mouse with a sharper snout and teeth so strong that it can cut through even harder materials as a saw does - whence, from "saw" (serra), it is called sorex, Isidore says.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 51] On the weasel
div.p: The weasel (mustela), Isidore says, is named as though mus longus, "long mouse," for telon in Greek means "long." It is a very cunning creature, and in the houses where it raises its young, it often moves them from place to place so that they may not be taken from it. It has less fear of cats, and it hunts mice. The male of this kind is called mygale, and when it grows old its whole coat turns white and becomes very valuable. Before fighting a serpent, the weasel eats rue, as Macer says, and once it has killed the serpent, it goes to water and purifies itself. The weasel alone kills the viper and the basilisk. There are two kinds of weasel, Isidore says: one is domestic, which we call by the common name "weasel"; the other is wild, larger in body and of a redder colour, less venomous, called by the Greeks ictis and by us specifically "marten," which preys not on serpents but on chicks and birds. Some fancifully claim that the weasel conceives through the mouth and gives birth through the ear, but this is false, as Aristotle and Isidore say.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 52] On the solifuga (shrew)
div.p: The shrew (musaraneum), according to Isidore, is the animal that Solinus calls solifuga. It is small in body, like a little mouse, but shaped like a spider, and is called solifuga because it flees the sun and daylight; musaraneum comes from mus ("mouse") and aranea ("spider"). It is found in Sardinia and creeps about above all in the silver mines, and whoever happens to sit upon it, or touches it with a bare hand, is killed by its venom, as Solinus says.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 53] On the spider
div.p: The spider, Aristotle says, is an animal devoted to constant labour and toil. It disembowels itself, so to speak, drawing threads out from its own substance and, once thickened in the surrounding air, spins them and makes for itself, on walls, a web like a net, so that flies or ants falling into it become caught by their feet; hence it always makes two webs, one in which it lives, another in which it catches flies and ants. It is a very venomous creature, harmful in its bite, so much so that it can even bring death to other venomous animals. It is named, according to Isidore, from aer, "air," because it makes its web from the nourishment of the air; or it is called aranea as though arcens ranam, "warding off the frog," for the frog flees its poison. The spider kind, as will become clear below, is reckoned among the worms.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 54] On the mole
div.p: The mole, Isidore holds, is named because it is condemned to blindness. It has no eyes, yet has something like eyes beneath its skin, as Aristotle says, as though nature had meant to give it eyes and then withheld them, judging them of no use to it. It is an animal that always remains in the earth, eating earth, and it digs out furrows and mounds; whence the verse: "the earth nourishes the mole," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 55] On the dormouse
div.p: The dormouse (glis, gen. gliris), Isidore says, is a certain small animal named from gliscere, "to crave" or "to grow." It takes great delight in sleeping, for it is then that it grows and fattens greatly. It sleeps the whole winter through, lying as if half-dead, but comes back to life in the summer season.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 56] On the cricket
div.p: The cricket (grillus) is a very small animal that hides in the walls of houses, and takes its name from the sound of its call, for it sings constantly. It walks backward and bores into the earth, and above all chirps at night. The ant is its enemy and hunts it in this way: the ant ties a hair around itself and casts it into the cricket's burrow, first clearing away all the loose earth so that the cricket cannot hide, and so, entangled in that hair, draws the cricket out.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 57] On the ant
div.p: The ant, Isidore says, is named as though ferens micas farris, "carrying crumbs of grain." It is an animal that provides for itself and labours with great diligence: in summer it lays up provisions for the whole winter, and at harvest time gathers only wheat, never touching barley; and if by chance rain should wet one grain of the wheat it has stored, it casts that grain out at once, knowing that it will rot and spoil the rest along with it. Whence Solomon says: "go to the ant, O sluggard, and imitate her ways, and be wiser than she." Ambrose says a sign of fair weather may be read from ants in this way: when a whole day is going to be fair, the ants carry all the heaps they have gathered out into the sun and there purify and dry them. Solinus says that on the borders of Ethiopia there are ants shaped like dogs, which dig golden sand out of the earth with their feet and guard what they have dug up so fiercely that they will pursue to the death anyone who tries to take it.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 58] On the ant-lion
div.p: The ant-lion (formicoleon), Isidore says, is an animal of the same kind and shape as the ant, but larger and stronger, and it preys upon ants, for it hides itself in the dust along their path and, when ants come by carrying grain, attacks and kills them. Hence it is named formicoleon, from formica ("ant") and leo ("lion"), because it is, as it were, a lion to ants and an ant to other, larger animals. Blessed Gregory mentions this creature in his Moralia [on Job].

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 59] On the hedgehog
div.p: The hedgehog, Isidore says, is a spiny, bristly animal with a snout much like a pig's, and is named from erigere, "to raise up," because it raises its spines when threatened; and whenever it senses any danger, it at once curls up, drawing in its feet, and rolls its snout into a ball. Its cunning is this: when it seeks to carry grapes from the vine or fruit from a tree back to its den, it rolls itself into a ball and tumbles among the fallen fruit or grapes on the ground, and whatever sticks to it in this way it carries off to its den upon its spines. It preys on serpents: when it seizes one, it wraps itself around the serpent's head and holds it immovably, and meanwhile the struggling serpent dashes itself against the hedgehog's spines, and so, worn down by its own thrashing, is at last overcome and dies. Ambrose says the hedgehog keeps its den closed on every side except for two small openings which it leaves for breathing, one facing north, which it stops up in winter, the other facing south, which it closes in summer - so that one of the two is always open, but each in its proper and fitting season.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 60] On the wisent (bison)
div.p: The wisent, Solinus says, is a wild beast found only in the forests of Germany, of the size and shape of an ox, having large and handsome horns, but with bristles on its neck and a great mane. They are fierce and untamable, and do not grow gentle even when captured.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 61] On the elk
div.p: The elk, Solinus says, is a certain wild animal born only in the forests of Germany, of the size and bodily shape of a mule, and has an upper lip so prominent and projecting beyond the lower that it can never eat except while sitting back on its hind legs.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 62] On the ceffa
div.p: The ceffa, Solinus says, is a certain animal born in Ethiopia, which has front feet like a man's hands, but hind feet resembling human feet.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 63] On the catoblepas
div.p: The catoblepas, the same Solinus says, is a certain animal likewise born in Ethiopia; it is a sluggish, modest-sized beast with a large head and a gaze so pestilential and deadly that whoever looks into its eyes dies at once.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 64] On the parandrus
div.p: The parandrus, Solinus says, is a certain beast the size of an ox, with cloven feet, branching horns, a head like a stag's, the colour and teeth of a bear, and shaggy fur. This animal, Solinus says, has this peculiar nature: when it flees, afraid, during a hunt, it takes on the colour of whatever it draws near, and for this reason is difficult to catch. The octopus does the same in the sea, and the chameleon on land, of which we spoke above. Solinus says that this changing of colour, according to what it approaches, is produced by the polish and sheen of its fur, as though it were a kind of mirror.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 65] On the manticore
div.p: The manticore, Solinus says, is a certain animal in India, having three rows of teeth in each jaw, a face like a man's, grey-blue eyes and an entirely blood-red colouring, a lion's body, and also a stinging tail like a scorpion's, and a voice so shrill that it seems almost to sing like a pipe. It greatly craves human flesh. It runs and leaps so swiftly that nothing can catch up with it when it flees.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 66] On the phalangium (venomous spider)
div.p: The phalangium, Solinus says, is a certain small creature in Crete, shaped and sized like a spider, whose venom is so overwhelming that, as Solinus says, if you ask after the strength or size of this creature's body, there is none to speak of; but if you ask after its power, it can kill a man with a single sting of its venom.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 67] On the hyena
div.p: The hyena, Solinus says, is a certain animal in Africa, having stiff, upright bristles, but a neck so inflexible that it cannot turn it at all without turning its whole body along with it. This animal follows shepherds' folds by night and, listening carefully, learns and remembers some voice or name from them, and then, lying hidden in ambush, calls out to a man by uttering that same voice, and kills him when he comes. It also mimics and imitates human vomiting and sobbing, and by this lures dogs to itself, kills them, and devours them. If hunting dogs so much as touch its shadow, they can no longer bark. It digs up the bones of the dead from their graves and carries them off. Its eyes have many colours, and it changes those same colours at will.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 67, note] The hyena-stone
div.p: In the pupil of its eye is found a stone called the hyaenus, which, if placed beneath the tongue of a sleeping person, foretells the future, as is said in the Lapidary. Whatever animal the hyena has circled three times can no longer move at all, and for this reason magicians and enchanters believed this animal to possess a power of divination.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 68] On the crocotta
div.p: The hyena, Solinus says, sometimes mates with a lioness, and from this union is born a certain animal called the crocotta. This animal likewise learns to mimic human voices; its gaze and the movement of its eyes never rest still. It has no tongue in its mouth, and only a single tooth, which is enclosed in a kind of case so that it will not be dulled by excessive use, but remains always sharp.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 69] On the bonnacon
div.p: The bonnacon, Solinus says, is a certain animal born in Asia Minor, having a head like a bull's, and the rest of its body covered somewhat like a horse's, with a mane; its horns are so flexible, and withal so soft, that if anyone runs into them and strikes against them, they suffer no injury at all. It has, however, one means of defence: when it flees during a hunt, or flees having been otherwise wounded, it releases hot, liquid dung with such force, as if shot from a bow, that it reaches as far as three acres away, and whatever it touches it destroys equally by its stench and its burning heat.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 70] On the leucrota
div.p: The leucrota, Solinus says, is a certain animal in India, so swift that it outruns nearly every other beast; it is the size of a donkey, having haunches like a stag's, a chest and legs like a lion's, a head resembling a camel's, a cloven hoof, and a mouth opening all the way to its ears, with, in place of teeth, a single continuous ridge of bone. It also imitates the voice of a speaking man.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 71] On the yale
div.p: The yale, Solinus says, is a certain animal in India, likewise fabulous, shaped like a horse, with an elephant's tail, black in colour, having jaws that stretch wide open, and two horns longer than a cubit, flexible in any direction it wishes to turn them, yet very hard; it uses only one at a time, keeping the other in reserve for a time of need, so that once the first is blunted it can fight with the second. It lives on land and in water, like the hippopotamus, whence it is called by some the Indian hippopotamus.

div.head: [II, 2, 1, 72] Summary of the foregoing
div.p: The land animals, or walking creatures, listed above are the more notable and famous among the authorities, though there are far more of them, indeed almost countless, named even by Pliny, on which we need not dwell further at present. Among the land creatures there are also the creeping ones, which change place not by the motion of feet but by the contraction and extension of their vertebrae and rings, not walking but crawling, as serpents and worms do; of these something shall now be given by way of example, for the reader's pleasure, beginning generally with serpents.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 1] General discourse on serpents
div.p: Serpents, Isidore says, are named from serpere, "to crawl," since, as has been said, they do not walk but crawl; and this is the general name for all creeping things. The word anguis, however, comes from angere, "to constrict," because by coiling and winding itself around, it constricts and chokes whatever it seizes. Coluber, again, is named because it "haunts the shade" (colit umbras); for although every kind of serpent, Isidore says, is by nature cold, they are nonetheless accustomed, for their own safety and protection, to frequent shady places even against their own nature. The kinds of serpents, Isidore says, are in a sense innumerable, for there are as many kinds of venom as there are kinds of serpent, as many forms of destruction as there are species, as many colours as there are torments they inflict.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 1, note] On the cold nature of serpents and their venom
div.p: All serpents, Isidore says, are cold by nature, and yet they harm only when warmed; when they are cold they touch no one, and for this reason their venom does more harm by day than by night. For they grow sluggish in the chill of night and have then nothing lively in them, since the cold of night increases their own coldness; for this same reason they withdraw in winter into the depths of the earth, which are then warmer, but in summer, as the heat returns over the face of the earth, they come back up to the surface. For this reason, too, warm lands are the nurseries of serpents, above all Africa and India, while cold lands are hostile to them; whence Solinus says that the soil of Ireland, that island of the western ocean, kills serpents wherever it is carried. That venom does no harm except when warmed and roused by heat is proven, Isidore says, by the fact that when someone is struck by venom, he first grows cold and numb, as it were, and only afterward, once the venom has reached the natural, blood-borne heat, is it at once strengthened by contact with that natural warmth, and that same heat is in turn further roused against the coldness of the venom and becomes disordered by its own intensity, and corruption and death follow.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 1, note 2] On venom and the sluggish senses of serpents
div.p: All venom, then, is cold, and "venom" (venenum) is named, according to Isidore, from venae, "veins," because it has no destructive effect until it reaches the veins, the vessels of the blood, which is hostile to venom - so that venom cannot harm unless it enters the veins and touches the blood, as Lucan says: "the harmful plague of serpents lies in the mingling of blood." Pliny says that a serpent's life resides so entirely in its head that, even if it should escape with only two fingers' worth of its body left, it will still live; hence it guards only its head, exposing all its other members in its place. All serpents, Solinus says, have dull sight, for they do not see well, having their eyes not in the front of the face but at the temples, and for this reason they can rarely see sideways, but hear more readily than they see. No animal moves its tongue with such speed as the serpent, so much so that to onlookers it sometimes seems to have three tongues, because of the swiftness of its motion. The bodies of serpents, Isidore says, are so moist that on level ground, where they crawl, they leave a track behind them. The manner of a serpent's crawling is this: it rests on its scales, by their sharpness, as if on feet, and on its ribs as if on legs, and contracts and extends itself by its vertebrae and rings, and so creeps or crawls. Serpents are very cunning, and fittingly so, for Aristotle says that bloodless animals are more resourceful than blooded ones - which perhaps is meant by what is said in Genesis, that the serpent was more cunning than all the other creatures upon the earth. Serpents live so long that, by shedding their old skin through the passage of some narrow opening, they renew both skin and age together; the skin thus shed is called the serpent's exuviae, "cast-off," and what it puts on anew, once renewed, is called its induvium, "new garment." Pythagoras says that a serpent can be generated from the marrow of a dead man; whence Ovid: "there are those who believe that when the spine has rotted in a sealed tomb, human marrow is changed into a serpent." Some say that the spittle of a fasting man kills a serpent. It is also said that a serpent does not dare touch a naked man, above all in water, and this seems plausible. Ambrose indeed says that many animals harmful on land are harmless in water. And common people say that the serpent lays down its venom in water - but this is not entirely true, except insofar as, as was said above, venoms have no power unless roused by some heat; and so, just as they harm less by night than by day, so too they harm less in water than on land. Ambrose says that a serpent, when it feels its eyesight growing weak, eats fennel, and is helped by this.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 2] On the dragon
div.p: The dragon, Isidore says, is the largest of all serpents, indeed of all land creatures, and the word is wholly Greek. This kind of serpent, Isidore says, is often carried through the air from its lair, and by its motion and size disturbs the whole sky. It is a winged serpent, with two front feet, crested, with a small mouth and narrow passages through which it draws breath, and it darts out its tongue; and for this reason its power lies not in its teeth but in its tail, and it does harm not by biting but by the blow of its tail. It has no venom, but is so large and powerful an animal that whatever it seizes with its tail it crushes and kills. The dragon preys upon the elephant, wrapping its tail around the elephant's legs and bringing it down, though it too is sometimes crushed beneath it, so that both die together. Solinus says that in the dragon's head is a most precious stone, called the dracontia gem, and it is not a true stone unless taken from a living dragon's head; once the dragon dies, it evaporates and vanishes. For this reason, men skilled in such matters in the regions of India take sleep-inducing herbs and make a compound from them, casting it before the dragons' lairs; and when the dragon tastes it, it begins to sleep, and so they approach and cut the stone from it while it sleeps.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 2b] On the basilisk
div.p: The basilisk, Isidore says, is interpreted as "king," because it is king of all serpents, since other serpents flee its venom. By its scent alone it kills men and birds flying above it in the air, by its gaze alone. It is overcome, however, by the weasel, which men send into its lairs, and which kills the serpent. It is only half a foot long, and marked with white spots. Solinus says the basilisk is deadly not only to living creatures but to the very earth over which it crawls, so that it kills and scorches the grasses and herbs through which it passes; other serpents fear its hiss. It crawls on the ground with the middle part of its body, while the rest, up to its head, stands erect. Whatever it kills with its bite, neither bird nor beast will touch.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 2b, note] On the remains of the basilisk
div.p: The remains of a slain basilisk put to flight all animals and venomous creatures, wherever they may be. Whence Solinus relates that the people of Cyrene hung the corpse of a basilisk in a golden net in the temple of Apollo, so that neither spider nor fly could weave its web there or dwell within the temple.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 3] On the regulus
div.p: The regulus, Isidore says, is a certain kind of serpent that readily crawls in dry, parched places, like the scorpion, and once it has come to water and then bitten someone, it makes him hydrophobic or frenzied. This same serpent is also called sibilus, "the hisser," because it kills with its hiss before it even touches or bites.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 4] On the viper
div.p: The viper, according to Isidore, is named because it gives birth "by force" (vi parit). There are never more than two vipers, a male and a female, at any time, and this comes about because, when the female viper is about to give birth, she has twins within her which, unable to wait for the proper time, gnaw through their mother's sides and come forth before their time, at the cost of their mother's death; whence Lucan: "the coils of the viper come together, its body torn open." It is said that when vipers mate, the male inserts his mouth into the female's mouth and spits his seed into her, and the female, driven to a frenzy by the heat of her desire, bites off the male's head - and this is why there are never more than two vipers at a time. From the remains of the viper are made medicinal lozenges called theriac, Isidore says. Others say the serpent from which theriac is made is a different one, called the tyrus, whence theriaca is named.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 5] On the asp
div.p: The asp, according to Isidore, is named from the harshness (asperitas) of its venom, or because by biting it "scatters" (spargit) its venom. There are many kinds of it, Isidore says, but the effects of its venom differ. The Observer says that when an asp begins to be affected by a snake-charmer's spell, it goes to a rock and presses one ear against the stone while stopping the other with its tail, so that it cannot hear the charmer's voice - for if it heard and did not come, it would burst at once. Whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "the cold snake in the meadow bursts from singing."

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 6] On the dipsas
div.p: The dipsas, Isidore and Solinus say, is a kind of serpent called in Latin situla, "the bucket." Whoever it bites will die of thirst.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 7] On the hypnalis
div.p: The hypnalis is a kind of serpent of the asp family, spoken of above, and is named, according to Isidore, because its venom kills men gently, as though putting them to sleep. Whence we read that Cleopatra applied this serpent to herself while sleeping, and died as though still asleep.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 8] On the haemorrhois
div.p: Haemorrhois in Greek means, in Latin, "flow of blood," and is the name of a certain serpent of the asp kind, as those described above. It is so named because whoever it bites will bleed entirely until he dies, Isidore says - for haima in Greek means "blood," whence Haemathia, that is, "bloody," was the name given to Thessaly on account of the wars fought there.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 9] On the prester
div.p: The prester, Isidore says, is a certain serpent that always keeps its mouth gaping open, breathing out venom; whence the poet: "the greedy prester, its steaming jaws stretched wide." Whomever this serpent strikes swells up throughout the whole body as if dropsical, and then dies as its humours putrefy.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 10] On the seps
div.p: The seps, Isidore says, is a serpent very venomous and wasting, so that whomever it strikes it consumes at once, so that he seems to melt away like wax in the serpent's very mouth.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 11] On the cerastes
div.p: The cerastes is a certain serpent, Isidore says, so named because it has two horns on its head, like a ram - for keras in Greek means "horns" in Latin. This serpent's horns are square, or fourfold, Isidore says, and with them it catches other animals by this device and cunning: it buries its whole body in the sand, leaving only its horns exposed, and when animals pass by, they stop, as if marvelling at these horns with no body attached; then the serpent, springing up behind them, bites and kills one of them. It is, Isidore says, more sinuous than other serpents, since it lacks a spine in its back; and of this serpent it is said in Genesis: "let Dan be a serpent in the way, a cerastes in the path," and so on - for the coluber, as was said above, is the name for serpents of this kind that lurk in the shadows, either for their own protection or so as to strike passers-by more easily.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 12] On the scytale
div.p: The scytale, Isidore says, is likewise a kind of serpent, which has upon itself so many varieties of colour that it turns onlookers, as it were, to stupefaction; and because it is slow, it detains men in their tracks more by the sight of it, as it crawls, than by pursuit or motion. It is, moreover, more naturally warm than other serpents, so much so that, contrary to the nature of other serpents, it sheds its skin even in winter. Of which Lucan says: "and the scytale alone, even now amid the scattered frosts, about to shed its skin," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 13] On the amphisbaena
div.p: The amphisbaena, Isidore says, is a serpent having two heads, one at the front and another at the tail, and for this reason it moves both forward and backward, and the reverse, in a circular motion of its body - that is, now forward, now back. This serpent, more than any other, dares to expose itself to the cold, for other serpents cannot well bear cold. Its eyes also gleam like a lamp. Of this Lucan says: "and the fearsome amphisbaena, bending toward its double head."

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 14] On the enhydris (water-snake)
div.p: The enhydris, Isidore says, is a certain serpent living in water, named from hydor, "water," and en, "in." Hence among the Greeks all water-serpents in general are called hydrae. Those struck by its bite all swell up, and the sickness that follows from this is called boas, because there is no remedy against it except cow dung bound over the site of the bite.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 15] On the hydra
div.p: The hydra is a dragon, or great water-serpent, of many heads, such as was perhaps the one in the Lernaean marsh of Arcadia, of which the fables say that Hercules killed it, and that when one head was cut off, seven grew back in its place. But in historical truth, this "Hydra" was a certain place in that region, spewing forth waters, so that when one channel was blocked, it would burst forth in seven, or more, other places; and seeing this, Hercules burned that place, and by this burning closed up the pores and channels from which the water of that place erupted - and this gave rise to the fable. Isidore says that in Latin this hydra is called excedra, because when one head was cut off, three grew back.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 16] On the chelydrus
div.p: The chelydrus is a certain serpent so named because it is both aquatic and terrestrial, for, as Isidore holds, chersos in Greek means "land," hydor "water." This serpent, in whatever part of the earth it slithers, leaves a smoking track behind it. Whence Macer: "whether its foaming back breathes out venom, or the earth smokes where the foul serpent glides." And Lucan: "and the smoking track left by the passing chelydrus." This serpent, Isidore says, always moves in a straight line, for if it bent itself, its whole body would burst.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 17] On the water-snake (natrix)
div.p: The natrix is a certain aquatic serpent, Isidore says, and it poisons water with its venom, so that whatever spring it enters it corrupts with poison. Whence Lucan: "and the natrix, defiler of the water," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 18] On the cenchris
div.p: The cenchris, Isidore says, is a serpent that never turns aside to either side, but always goes straight ahead. Whence Lucan: "and the cenchris, ever gliding along a straight path."

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 19] On the parias
div.p: The parias, Isidore says, is a certain serpent that always moves only by its tail, and for this reason, since the sharp tip of its tail furrows the ground, it always leaves a track behind it. Whence Lucan: "content to furrow its path with its tail alone, the parias."

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 20] On the boa
div.p: The boa, Solinus and Isidore say, is a serpent of astonishing size in Calabria, so large that it preys upon herds of cattle, killing and eating oxen; whence it took its name from boves, "oxen." It craves above all the milk of cattle and cows, Solinus says. It grows to such a size, Solinus says, that whole infants or men, swallowed into its belly, have often been found there once it was killed.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 21] On the jaculus
div.p: The jaculus is a flying serpent with certain small wings, Isidore says; of which Lucan writes: "and the flying jaculi." It flies from tree to tree, and if any animal, or even an armed man, should happen to be in its path, it pierces him through in the force of its flight and kills him. In Arabia, Solinus says, there are winged serpents called sirens, which run much faster than horses and are for this reason called winged or flying; their venom, Isidore says, is of such power that its victims die from a single strike even before they feel any pain.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 22] On the obytes
div.p: The obytes is a certain serpent, Isidore says, so named because it has the colour of sand along with its venom, and is by no means the least deadly. Of which the poet says: "the Tryphonian obytes, marked with such small spots, the same colour as the sun-scorched sand and indistinguishable from it."

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 23] On the dipsas (small kind) and related tiny serpents
div.p: There is another serpent called dipsas, of the same name but a different kind from the one named above, Solinus says, and it is so tiny that it cannot be seen underfoot, and yet its venom is so strong that its victim dies before even feeling the pain of the bite. Whence the poet: "the young standard-bearer Aulus, of Etruscan blood, trodden underfoot, was bitten by the dipsas, which twisted its head back; scarcely was there pain or any sense of the bite," and so on. The salpigna is likewise a kind of serpent that cannot be seen. The same creature is also called cecula, "the little blind one," because it has tiny eyes and neither sees nor is seen. There is also another kind of serpent called the centipede, named for its many feet; this may also serve as a general name for all serpents having many feet, which some call, more precisely, multipedes.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 24] On lizards, in general
div.p: The lizard (lacertus), Isidore says, is a kind of serpent, or rather of creeping thing, so named because it has lacerti, that is, "arms." The kinds of lizard, Isidore says, are three; according to Solinus, however, four: namely the frog-lizard (botraca), the salamander, the saura, and the stellio.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 25] On the botraca
div.p: The botraca is so named because it has a face like a frog's, for botrachos in Greek means "frog."

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 26] On the salamander
div.p: The salamander is likewise so named because it has power against fire. Indeed the force of its venom is such that it not only lives in fire but even extinguishes it. If it climbs a tree, it poisons all its fruit in an instant; if it falls into a well, it fatally poisons the whole of the water.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 27] On the saura
div.p: The saura, again, is a kind of lizard which, when it feels its eyesight weakening from old age, enters a hole in a wall facing east, and so, when the sun rises, has its sight restored by the light.

div.head: [II, 2, 2, 28] On the stellio
div.p: The stellio lives in houses around men and does them no harm; of which Solomon says: "the stellio supports itself on its hands and dwells in the houses of kings." It is of varied colour, marked with spots; whence Ovid, on this same creature: "it takes its name from the star-like spots scattered over its body, well suited to its colouring," and so on. It preys upon scorpions in this way: it inserts its tail into the scorpion's burrow, and when the scorpion has fastened onto it, draws it out of its den and devours it.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 1] On worms, in general
div.p: There is this difference, Isidore says, between serpents and worms: serpents are called the larger creeping things, which are generated through the mating of the two sexes, whereas worms are the smaller creeping things, which are born not through mating but out of putrefaction - for the heat of any given matter, once it begins to be drawn toward the surface by exterior warmth, begins there to persist a little, and out of this exterior heat acting upon a natural warmth arises, in that matter, the generative power of a soul: this is the manner in which worms are generated, as Aristotle says in the twelfth book of the Metaphysics, and the power of the heavens works upon putrefied matter in the same way that a father's power works in seed. More broadly speaking, however, Isidore says worms are not only those generated from putrefaction in the manner described, but also other tiny creeping things born from eggs, such as scorpions. The kinds of worms, then, are distinguished according to the different kinds of matter from whose putrefaction they are born, and for this reason, Isidore says, worms belong to air, water, or earth, among the class of simple bodies. Fire, however, generates no worms of its own, since, as Aristotle says in the fourth book of the Meteorology, fire does not putrefy, and for this reason no worms are generated from it - or else the generation of all worms may be attributed to fire's heat, since, as has been said, worms are generated in any matter through exterior heat. Among compound bodies, worms properly and chiefly belong to flesh, leaves, wood, or clothing, and we shall name these kinds in order; perhaps worms are generated from every kind of putrefied matter, but these are the most notable of all.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 2] On the spider (as a worm of air)
div.p: The spider, Isidore says, is a worm of the air, generated, that is, from the putrefaction of air, of which we spoke above.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 3] On the leech
div.p: The leech (sanguisuga or hirudo) is a worm born of the putrefaction of water, and is so named because it sucks (sugit) blood, and once it is full, vomits that blood back up so as to suck fresh blood again. Of which Horace says: "the leech that has once seized hold does not let go until it dies from gorging, and will not release its grip until it is full of blood."

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 4] On the scorpion
div.p: The scorpion, Isidore says, is a worm born from the putrefaction of earth in warm regions, shaped altogether like a crab, but with a stinging and very venomous tail, so that its sting kills unless a remedy is applied in time. It can only strike upward, since its stinger curves upward. Isidore says it does not harm the palm of the hand alone. Oil in which scorpions have putrefied is effective against a scorpion's sting and against other venomous bites and swellings.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 5] On the cantharis (blister-beetle)
div.p: The cantharis is likewise a worm of the earth, which, once attached to a man's body, clings on at once and, by its burning or its sting, raises blisters on people full of fluid.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 6] On the millipede
div.p: The millipede is likewise a certain worm, which is born under stones from the moisture of the earth. It is named for the multitude of its feet, and when disturbed rolls itself into a ball and lies hidden beneath the stones.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 7] On the slug
div.p: The slug (limax) is named a "worm of mud" (limus) because it is generated, in rainy weather, in muddy ground - a dirty and unclean worm which common folk call the "rain-worm," because they crawl up out of the earth in rainy weather.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 8] On the silkworm
div.p: The silkworm (bombex) is a worm of leaves, from whose spinning silken parchment [silk cloth] is made, Isidore says, and it is so named because it empties itself entirely in the weaving of its threads, so that it is left hollowed out, its skin filled with nothing but air.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 9] On the caterpillar
div.p: The caterpillar (eruca) is a worm of vegetables, wrapped in the leaves and tendrils of vines, and it consumes vegetables and vines; hence eruca is named from erodere, "to gnaw away." Of which the Prophet says: "what the locust left, the caterpillar ate," and so on. And Plautus: "imitating a worthless and harmful creature, wrapped up in a vine-leaf, it entangles itself."

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 10] On the woodworm
div.p: The teredo, called in Greek teredona, is the wood-worm, named in Latin interpretation from terebrare, "to bore," or termes from terere, "to wear away," because by boring small holes it consumes the whole piece of wood. These are generated in wood cut at the wrong time of year.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 10, note] Remedies against garden and wood pests
div.p: The remedy against caterpillars in vegetable gardens is the smell of sulphur scattered about the garden; against woodworms, timber should be carefully anointed with sulphur and vinegar.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 11] On the clothes-moth and other worms of the flesh
div.p: The moth (tinea) is the worm of clothing, named from tenere, "to hold," because it clings firmly to garments until it gradually consumes the threads and reduces the cloth to dust. The remedy against these is to place rue or wild mint among one's clothes, whose scent kills them. As for the worms of flesh: some are born within the body, from putrefied humours, others outside it, on the body's surface, from sweat and the excess matter of the outer skin. Of those born within the body, some are born in the head or gums, and this worm is called the migraine-worm, from a certain membrane of the brain which it especially damages; others form in the intestines, and these are called lumbrici, as though "slippery ones" (lubrici), or from lumbi, "loins," because they especially afflict the loins. These worms are born, Aristotle says in the fourth book of the Meteorology, not in the mouth of the stomach but in the lower belly, where the further digestion of food takes place - for the first digestion, which occurs in the stomach, is not, Aristotle says, complete enough there to introduce life through its own putrefactions, and for this reason intestinal worms never come out through the mouth in vomit, however much certain tricksters and frauds pretend otherwise, since nothing can come out in vomit except what is in the mouth of the stomach. Those born on the outside of the body are these: the ascarides, or costi, or lice (pediculi, named from the multitude of "feet," pedes), and fleas (pulices), named because they are generated in summer from the warm dust of the earth clinging to bodies, and nits (lendes), named because they bite with a lighter sting. The ascarides are very small worms between skin and flesh, which cause itching with their bites. The tarmus is the worm found in lard or cheese. The ricinus is a worm that settles chiefly in dogs' ears and causes itching there. The ustia is a worm of pigs, so named because it consumes the flesh with its bite as if burning it, and swelling and blistering follow. The bedbug (cimex), however, is a worm properly born in rotting flesh, so named from a certain herb whose smell it shares.

div.head: [II, 2, 3, 11, note] Remedies against household pests
div.p: Against lice: let a man wear a belt dyed with sulphur. Against fleas: scatter wormwood steeped in vinegar on the floor. Against worms in cheese or meat: apply wild mint. Against flies: place ground orpiment mixed with vinegar on a stone in the house.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 1] On fish, in general
div.p: Following the earlier division according to the elements in which they live, the kind of animals that live in water are called aquatic, and these are called fish (pisces) from pastus or pascere, "to feed," Isidore says, because they are of most pleasing flavour to eat, though some fish provide little nourishment. The kinds of fish are less known to land animals [i.e. to us], and for this reason, Isidore says, they received their names later, from various occasions and causes - either from a resemblance to land animals, as the frog-fish, the calf-fish, the lion-fish, the blackbird-fish, the peacock-fish and the thrush-fish; or from a change of habit, as the dog-fish and wolf-fish, so named for their resemblance in voracity; or from colour, as the umbra and the gilthead (which has a golden head), and the "varied" fish, named for the variety of its colouring, commonly called trout; or from shape and form, as a certain fish called the "round one" (orbis) for its roundness, and the sword-fish (gladiolus), because its shape resembles a sword. Which class of animals as a whole is prior by nature or in creation - the land, the water, or the flying creatures - is a matter of doubt. Aristotle, however, says that blooded creatures are by nature prior to the bloodless, and according to him this is the essential division and difference among the whole classes of animals in relation to one another. Ambrose says that the aquatic creatures were prior in creation to the others. Aquatic animals in general are also called creeping things (reptilia), but there are, according to Isidore and Ambrose, two kinds of them: some are swimmers, which live and swim only in water and die outside it, as most kinds of fish; others are amphibious, that is, of a doubtful class, Isidore says, since they live both in water and on land, swimming in the one and walking in the other, such as the seal, the crocodile, and the hippopotamus. Fish, Ambrose says, cannot live without water for this reason: that which the breathing in and out of air provides to land animals - moderating and tempering their natural heat by way of the windpipe, through the chest, to the lungs - is provided to fish by the passage of water through certain fine channels at the gills; for although they have, according to Aristotle, no blood and no lungs, they nonetheless have something in place of blood and lungs, and so, just as land creatures cannot live without air but are suffocated and die, so too aquatic creatures cannot live without water. The kinds of fish, Ambrose says, are distinguished thus: some lay eggs, which, once rubbed off onto the sand and fertilised by the milt cast over them by the male fish, become fish in time - for they do not brood over them as birds do. Others bear their young alive, as the sea-weasel (mustela) and the dogfish (canicula) among fish, and dolphins and seals; and this egg-laying kind of fish has no nests or fixed dwellings in the water. Those that bear live young, however, have their own nests and dwellings, Ambrose says, and this kind mates with none but its own species. Some fish, Ambrose says, eat earth, others grass, others gnats and ants and water-frogs; some among them live by plunder, and the larger eats the smaller of its own kind or of another, as the pike and the catfish do. Every kind of fish that lives chiefly by plunder has two rows of teeth, upper and lower, so as more easily to seize and hold its prey. No kind of fish chews the cud, Ambrose says, except the parrotfish (scarus) alone. He also says that every kind of fish has its own distinct region of the water, and each kind keeps to its own region without straying beyond it. Certain kinds of fish, Ambrose says, change their location in the water not out of restlessness or inconstancy, but out of the necessity of tending their young. Every kind of large sea fish travels, in summertime, toward the northern sea, above all toward the Black Sea (Pontus), on account of the sweetness of the waters of that sea, for many freshwater rivers flow into that sea from the north, and the sun, too, passes briefly over that sea, so its waters are sweeter. All sea fish have tougher skin, on account of the sea's saltiness, which cannot penetrate them, and they are healthier to eat, because the salt water strips away all their sliminess. In summer, fish in all waters move toward colder places, and in winter return to warmer ones, Ambrose says. Great fish such as whales and cetaceans are found chiefly in the Atlantic Ocean, Ambrose says, on account of the depth of that sea. Fish, Ambrose says, have gills and a tail for this reason: with their gills they swim in the water and raise themselves up, while with their tail they turn themselves up and down and steer their course, as with an oar, in whatever direction they wish. Ambrose says that all kinds of fish named after land animals, which are venomous or harmful on land, are wholesome and edible in the water - as with the lion, on land and at sea, and the dog, on land and at sea, and the moray eel, and the frog. All venomous creatures, such as the serpent, and foul-smelling ones, such as the weasel, are improved once they enter water, Ambrose says, and for this reason few or none of the creatures that live in water are venomous, since venom requires the arousing heat that makes it harmful, and it is deprived of that heat in water - and for this reason, Isidore says, venomous things do little harm in water, as was said above.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 2] On the whale (balaena)
div.p: The balaena, Isidore says, is a great fish of the sea, and this fish conceives by means of a certain small fish which, from its resemblance to a weasel, is called the musculus. This fish is called balaena because, by the great size of its body, it makes the waters boil as it turns and rolls. Solinus says this kind of fish is found chiefly in the Indian Ocean, and the size of its body, once cast up on shore by fishermen, occupies a space of four acres. In the water, when approaching sailors, they raise themselves up beyond the yards and masts of ships, and have long, tube-like snouts with which they draw up seawater and pour it down upon the ships as if in a great flood of rain, and by this they try to sink the sailors.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 3] On the cetus (sea-monster)
