div.p: The cetus is a huge fish of the sea, found especially in the Atlantic Ocean, so large, Isidore says, that the size of its body resembles a mountain - such was the cetus that swallowed Jonah, of whom it is said: "out of the belly of hell you delivered me."

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 4] On sea-horses
div.p: Sea-horses are different from those called hippopotami, found in the river Nile. Sea-horses, Isidore says, are fish in their front part, but their whole hind part takes the shape of a horse. These are found in the ocean, whereas hippopotami are found only in the Nile.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 5] On seals (bocce)
div.p: The bocce, according to Isidore, are called "sea-oxen," as though boacce. Others call them seals (focae), or "sea-blue oxen," from the marine colour they display, that is, black mixed with green. This kind is amphibious, and in rainy weather they come out of the sea and dwell on land, around or in freshwater rivers. Ambrose says that once they have borne their young, they love and guard them greatly, and when they sense their young are about to be attacked by fishermen or other sea-beasts, they take them, unharmed, into their own mouths with their teeth and hold them there until the danger has passed; and if necessary, they even swallow them for a time and afterward bring them up safely again.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 6] On dolphins
div.p: The dolphin is, in the sea, a four-footed animal [in the sense of a mammal], about which Aristotle reports much. Isidore says this animal is so named because it follows the voices of men, and men gladly hear them and dwell alongside them, and dolphins show great affection toward them; whence Statius: "in the waters of Neptune no creature has such beauty of form, such power of swimming, nor more of a human heart." They gladly listen to music, Isidore says, and come, as it were, in schools to hear it. It is the swiftest of all sea creatures, so much so that it leaps clean over ships and their masts. When they leap and play among the waves, they signal an approaching storm. These, Isidore says, are also called simones. Solinus says there are many dolphins in the Hellespontine Sea, and that the Mediterranean, apart from dolphins and seals, has few large sea-creatures. At mating time the females wander off and bear their young in the tenth month, and only in summer. They suckle their young at the breast and, while still tender, carry them in their jaws. They also live thirty years. Their mouth is not placed as in other animals, but almost on the belly. Among all aquatic creatures, the dolphin alone moves its tongue. On its back it has spiny fins, which it raises when angered, but which otherwise lie flat and lowered. They do not breathe in water but in air. Their voice is like a human groan. They hear better when the north wind blows; when the south wind blows, they hear nothing at all. Solinus relates that a certain dolphin so befriended a boy that it took food from the boy's hand, and afterward the boy, whenever he wished, would sit upon the dolphin, which often carried him across the sea from one city to another; and later, when the boy died, the dolphin, grieving beside his funeral, died along with him from sorrow. He also tells of another dolphin, upon which a boy was sitting and playing in the sea when a storm arose, and the boy fell from the dolphin's back and drowned; the dolphin, taking up the drowned boy, carried him back to shore, and as if repenting its fault, never returned to the sea again, but died beside the shore of grief. When a dolphin bears young, the strongest of them all is chosen and made leader of the dolphin school in the sea, and the mother teaches him to guard the school against the ambushes of other sea-beasts.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 7] On tuna
div.p: The tunny (thynnus), Isidore says, is a Greek word, and it is a sea creature. These, Solinus says, are found only in the Black Sea (Pontus), and can breed nowhere else, on account of the sweetness of the waters of the Black Sea, which comes from the very cold northern waters that flow into that sea. They enter the sea in springtime to spawn, and do so along the right-hand shore; they leave, however, by the left, and this is because they see more sharply with the right eye than with the left.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 8] On the sea-pig (porpoise)
div.p: The suillus, Isidore says, is a four-footed sea creature, commonly called by the people the "sea-pig," and they are called "pigs" from this resemblance: that in seeking their food in the sea, they dig up and root through the seabed with their snouts, after the manner of pigs; this is because they chew not in the mouth but in the throat, and so cannot take or hold their food unless they thrust their snout into the sand or the mud of the water. These are good to eat and very fat.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 9] On the sea-raven
div.p: The corvus, Isidore says, is a certain sea creature, so named from the resemblance of its cry, for it has a voice like a crow's (corvus). It often grunts in the sea, and by this cry it is betrayed and caught.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 10] On the sword-fish
div.p: The gladiolus, Isidore says, is a certain sea fish, so named because it is shaped like a sword. It has two extended gills and a long, hard, extremely sharp snout, with which it pierces ships in the sea by charging at them with its snout.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 11] On the saw-fish
div.p: The saw-fish (serra) is likewise a sea fish, Isidore says, so named because it has a hard, saw-toothed crest along its back from head to tail, and by swimming beneath ships it cuts and saws through them.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 12] On the scorpaena
div.p: The scorpaena, Ambrose says, is a creature found in sea-marshes, shaped like a frog, but with a head resembling a serpent's. It is enclosed within two very hard shells, out of which it sometimes raises only its head and feet, and when it wishes, draws itself entirely back within them.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 12, note] Catching the scorpaena, and its nature
div.p: Isidore says that if someone ties ten crabs together with a bundle of basil and places them where scorpaenae are found, all the scorpaenae will gather to that spot. This creature lays eggs, Ambrose says, and mates with none but its own kind, and is named scorpaena from a certain resemblance to the land scorpion, though it has no venom, even though it is not of much use as food.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 13] On the sea-spider
div.p: The aranea, Isidore says, is a kind of fish, so named not from the spider-worm but from auris, "ear," as though auranea, because it has sharp, stinging spines around its ears, with which it wounds, and whatever it seizes with them will stick fast.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 14] On the crocodile
div.p: The crocodile is an animal living both on land and in the waters of the river Nile, Isidore and Solinus say. It is a four-footed creature, so named from its saffron colour, twenty or thirty cubits in length. It has no tongue, and moves only its upper jaw; it has two rows of extremely sharp teeth, and whatever it bites it crushes at once. It also has large and very sharp claws. By night it lives in the water, by day on land. Its hide is so tough that it withstands every blow without injury. It lays eggs like a goose's, and the male and female take turns brooding over them on alternate days. It seeks out a nesting place where the rising Nile cannot reach. Solinus says there is a kind of dolphin in the Nile with a very sharp, saw-toothed back; these attack crocodiles by swimming beneath them and pierce and kill them in the belly, where the skin is more tender. He also says that on an island in the Nile there are certain very small men, so spirited and bold that they attack and kill crocodiles - for it is the crocodile's nature to attack a fleeing man or animal, but if one stands its ground, the crocodile flees at once. The fish called the saw-fish also cuts and kills the crocodile at the belly.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 15] On the hippopotamus
div.p: The hippopotamus is likewise an animal found in the river Nile, shaped like a horse - for hippopotamus is interpreted as "river-horse." It is, Isidore says, like a horse in back, mane and neigh, but has a snub, upturned snout, tusks like a boar's, two hooves on each foot, and a curved tail. By day it stays in the water, but by night it grazes on the crops, entering the fields backward so that its tracks cannot be found and an ambush laid for it on its return. When it has grown too heavy from overeating, it rolls itself among sharp reeds until its legs bleed, and by this loss of blood becomes lighter; afterward it smears the wound with mud and heals it.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 16] On the sea-bream (pagrus)
div.p: The pagrus, Isidore says, is a certain sea fish, which the Greeks call phagrus, that is, "devourer." It has teeth so strong and sharp that it crushes oysters, however hard their shells, and lives on nothing but these for food.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 17] On the dentex
div.p: The dentex, Isidore says, is likewise a certain fish, so named because it has many strong teeth, and for this reason it lives only on the prey of small sea fish.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 18] On the sea-hare
div.p: The "hare" (lepus), Isidore says, is a certain fish, so named because it has a head resembling a hare's. It is, Ambrose says, a predatory fish, living by plunder, and whomever it bites suffers an incurable corruption of the flesh.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 19] On the sea-wolf
div.p: The "wolf" (lupus) is a certain fish, according to Isidore, so named for its rapacity, being very voracious and cunning in catching other fish. When it is surrounded by fishermen's nets, it opens the sand with its tail and, burrowing beneath, escapes.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 20] On the mullet
div.p: The mullet (mullus), Isidore says, is a certain fish so named as though mollis, "soft," because it has soft, tender flesh. Eaten, this fish restrains desire but dulls the eyes, and men who eat it often will, according to the fish's nature, smell of it themselves.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 20, note] On wine and the mullet
div.p: Whoever drinks wine in which a mullet has been drowned will afterward have an aversion to wine.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 21] On the grey mullet
div.p: The grey mullet (mugil) is so named, according to Isidore, as though "agile" (agilis). It is very swift in the water and cunning, so that when it senses fishermen's traps and nets, it darts backward so swiftly that it seems almost to fly.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 22] On the melanurus
div.p: The melanurus, Isidore says, is a fish so named from the Greek melan, "black," because it has a black tail, black gills, and scales marked with black lines.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 23] On the glaucus
div.p: The glaucus fish is so named, according to Isidore, from its colour, being whitish; in Greek this colour is called glaukeon. This fish, Isidore says, hides itself constantly during summer on account of fishermen, and rarely appears except on overcast days.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 24] On the grayling
div.p: The grayling (thymallus), Isidore and Ambrose say, takes its name from "flower" - for thymos in Greek means "flower." It is so named because it is most pleasing in appearance, smell and taste alike, both to look at and to eat; whence Ambrose: "it smells either of fish or of flower, for the scent of the fish and of the flower is the same."

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 25] On the parrotfish
div.p: The parrotfish (escarus), according to Isidore, is so named because it alone among fish chews the cud; Ambrose calls it scarus. It is very cunning at escaping when caught: for when trapped in a net, it does not try to force its way out head-first as other fish do, but with a blow of its tail loosens and widens the mesh of the net, and so slips out backward - and if another parrotfish sees it escaping in this way, it helps by seizing it with its teeth by the tail.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 26] On the sparus
div.p: The sparus, according to Isidore, is so named from the throwing-spear called in Greek sparon, because it is shaped like one - the fish having taken its name, as with other fish, from some more familiar thing it resembles.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 27] On the australis
div.p: The australis fish, according to Isidore, is named either from haurire, "to draw up," because it constantly draws up the waves of water with its open mouth, or from auster, "south wind," because it begins to appear more often when the south wind blows, at the setting of the Pleiades.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 28] On the amia
div.p: The amia, Isidore says, is a certain rock-fish, marked on its sides with reddish streaks amid a certain variegated grey colouring, and is named amia as though hamio, "by the hook," because it is sometimes caught not by net but by hook (hamus).

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 29] On the remora
div.p: The remora, Isidore and Ambrose say, is a small fish, half a foot long, so named because it makes ships come to a stop by swimming beneath them, through some hidden power of nature, so that the ship seems, as it were, rooted to the seabed. For this reason the Latins called it mora, "delay." Ambrose says the remora somehow senses and foretells a coming storm, for as a storm approaches it fears being cast up onto the sand by the waves; whence it rolls a small pebble before itself and holds it in its mouth, so that, aided by its weight, it will not be cast ashore.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 30] On the stargazer fish
div.p: The uranoscopus, Isidore says, is a certain fish, named from the Greek ouranos, "sky," and skopos, "to watch," hence uranoscopus, "watching the sky." It has a single eye, with which it always looks upward.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 31] On the flying fish
div.p: The myllago, Isidore says, is a certain fish so named because it often flies up out of the water. Whence fishermen say that when it leaps above the water more often than usual, it foretells a storm.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 32] On the dogfish (squatus)
div.p: The squatus is a certain fish, according to Isidore, named because it is exceedingly scaly, covered with sharp scales, so much so that its stripped skin is useful for polishing wood and other materials.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 33] On the sarra
div.p: The sarra, Isidore says, is a certain fish that abounds greatly near the Syrian city called Tyre, which was once called Sarra after the name of this fish; whence small fish resembling it are also called sarrae.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 34] On herring
div.p: The herring (allec) is a fat, pleasant-tasting fish, Isidore says, named, as it were, from lac, "milk." It abounds chiefly where the waters entering the sea toward England converge, and especially at the mouths of the Rhine to the north. It is so fat that salting preserves it a long time, and the people of that region use its fresh fat in lamps and wicks, as if it were oil, or in cooking food, as dripping. It is said that this fish lives only on the thicker, coarser matter suspended in the water, having no other food, and for this reason there is such abundance of this fish, owing to the abundance and constant presence of its nourishment, that even on feast days and days of rest, during the season when these fish appear - which happens once a year - the inhabitants of that region draw them out of the water. Of this the verse says: "the wave nourishes the herring," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 35] On the aphya (anchovy)
div.p: The aphya is a certain small fish, according to Isidore, so named from a, "without," and phoros, "carrying," because, owing to its smallness, it cannot be drawn up and taken out of the water on a hook.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 36] On the eel
div.p: The eel, Isidore and Solinus say, is so named from its resemblance to a serpent (anguis). It is a slippery, slimy fish, of little use to eat. It is born only in muddy waters and marshes, and cannot live in fresh, clean water. It is so slippery that the harder it is gripped, the more quickly it slips from the hand. If it is placed, along with a naked man or another animal, into fresh water, it flees the water at once by entering the man's anus. Solinus says that in the river Ganges of eastern India there are eels thirty feet long. Isidore says that whoever drinks wine in which eels have been drowned will thereafter have an aversion to drinking wine.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 37] On the sea-dragon
div.p: The sea-dragon is a certain fish, Isidore says, so named because it has venom, not for any resemblance in shape. This fish has, on its gills, spines curving toward the tail, with which, when it stings, it injects its venom at once.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 38] On the moray eel
div.p: The moray eel, Isidore and Ambrose say, is a certain fish, called in Greek smyraina, because it coils itself into a circle like a serpent - whence women's necklaces are also called murenulae. The Song of Songs says: "we will make you golden necklaces (murenulae)," and so on. This fish is entirely female, Ambrose says, and the male viper, by hissing along the shore, calls the moray eel out of the water and mates with it, and the moray eel thereby conceives, not a viper, but a moray eel; and for this reason, Isidore says, it is also called to the shore by fishermen imitating the serpent's hiss, and so is caught. It cannot be killed by a blow or with clubs, but dies at once when struck with a light rod. Its vital force lies chiefly in its tail and least of all in its head; hence an injury to the head does it no harm, but a touch to the tail kills it instantly.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 39] On the octopus
div.p: The polypus, Greek for what in Latin is called congrus, is so named, according to Isidore, from its multitude of feet - it is a fish having many feet, whence in Latin it is also called multipes, "many-footed." It is so cunning, Isidore says, that when a hook baited for it is thrown to it, it seizes the hook with its arms and holds it fast until it has gnawed away the whole bait, and only then releases the hook. Ambrose says this fish hunts other fish in this way: it goes in the water to some rock resembling itself in colour and attaches itself to it, so that there is no visible distance between itself and the rock, and passing fish, unable to distinguish it from the rock, are thus caught by it.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 40] On the electric ray
div.p: The torpedo, Isidore says, is a certain sea fish, so named because if anyone touches it while it is alive, his limbs begin to grow so numb (torpere) that he can move neither hands nor feet. Pliny says that in the Indian Ocean there are torpedoes whose very shadow renders men motionless; they produce the same effect even if touched only by means of a rod or staff.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 41] On the cuttlefish
div.p: The cuttlefish (sepia) is a certain fish, according to Isidore, so named because it shuts itself in among the hedges (sepes) of the water; this fish conceives through the mouth, like the viper. The Observer says that if cuttlefish fat is used in a lamp in place of oil, once the lamp is lit, everyone in the house will appear black, like Ethiopians.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 42] On the squid
div.p: The squid (lulligo) is a certain sea fish, Isidore says. This kind of fish exists in such numbers in the ocean off Mauretania, around the river Lixus, that when they rise up together out of the sea they can even sink ships.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 43] On the kinds of shellfish, in general
div.p: Shells and snails, Isidore says, are so named as though concava, "hollow," and this is the general name for all sea or land creatures enclosed within some kind of shell. They are named, according to Isidore, from their hollowness, because all animals enclosed in shells grow at the full moon and shrink as the moon wanes, since their shells become hollowed out and, as it were, emptied. There are many kinds of these, whose more notable ones we shall name in order.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 44] On the pearl-oyster
div.p: The pearl-oyster is a certain kind of shellfish, Isidore says, called by another name eceleoe, because it often goes to the shore and there takes in the dew of heaven, and from that dew the pearl gem is formed within its shell.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 45] On the murex
div.p: The murex, Isidore says, is a kind of shellfish, called by another name conchylium. It is named murex from the sharpness and roughness of its shell. From its shell a certain reddish-purple fluid is pressed out, called ostrum, from which red purple dye is made - and it is called ostrum because it is pressed out (exprimitur) from the shell (testa)'s fluid. These murex shells abound around the city of Pontus called Abydos; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "the Black Sea, and the straits of oyster-bearing Abydos, are tried," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 46] On the crab
div.p: The crab (cancer), Isidore says, is so named from its legs (crura), for among the shellfish it has legs and arms, which are called chelae; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "the place between Erigone and the pursuing Claws (Chelae)." The crab, Ambrose says, is an enemy of the oyster, and devours it in this way: it watches for when the oyster opens the shell of its housing, and then approaches stealthily and inserts a small pebble into the oyster's opening so that it can no longer close its shell, and so, entering, gnaws away its flesh. Isidore says that if someone ties ten crabs together with a bundle of basil in a house, all the scorpions in that house will gather to that spot.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 46, note] The crab's transformation and kinds
div.p: Pythagoras used to say that a living crab, its claws cut off and buried in the earth, turns into a scorpion within thirty days. Whence Ovid: "if you take away the hollow claws of the shore-crab, a scorpion will emerge, threatening with its curved tail." The crab alone, among the kinds of animals, moves backward, and this is because its effort in moving lies in the serrations of its tail, which are turned toward the rear. There are two kinds of crabs, namely sea crabs and those living in fresh water, and of these latter some live in rivers, others in marshes.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 47] On the oyster
div.p: The oyster, Isidore says, is so named in Greek as though "soft" (mollis), because its flesh is very soft, though its outer shell is extremely hard. The shell itself (ostreum) is of neuter gender, but its flesh is called ostrea, in the feminine; and the whole oyster kind is entirely female.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 48] On the mussel
div.p: The mussel (musculus), according to Isidore, is a certain kind of sea-shell, from whose milt the oyster conceives, just as the moray eel conceives from the viper; and hence mussels are named as though "males" (masculi). They are also called Pelorides, from Pelorus, a promontory of Sicily where they abound greatly; whence the poet: "and see, the North Wind from the narrow seat of Pelorus," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 49] On "nails" (razor clams)
div.p: The "nails" (ungues) are also a kind of shellfish, so called because they resemble human fingernails.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 50] On the tortoise
div.p: The tortoise, according to Isidore, is named as though tegmine teste opertus, "covered with the covering of a shell," in the manner of a kind of vaulted chamber. It is the slowest-moving of all animals that move from place to place. Among the shellfish, indeed, there are many that do not move from place to place at all, but merely drift here and there on the water's currents, and this is because their food is always present to them, so that they have no need of movement to obtain it. The kinds of tortoise, Isidore says, are four: land, sea, mud, and marsh tortoises. Of these, the sea tortoises are more useful for eating. The fat of every kind of tortoise is suited for ointments against the contraction of the sinews. Isidore says that a ship on board which the right foot of a tortoise is carried will travel much more slowly. Not all tortoises are of the same shape: some sea tortoises are entirely enclosed in long sheaths shaped like a finger, others in round shells. The flesh of tortoises greatly provokes desire.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 51] On the sea-urchin
div.p: The sea-urchin (icinus), Isidore says, is a certain kind of shellfish, which takes its name from the land icinus, that is, the hedgehog (ericius), for it is shaped like a hedgehog, having a spiny, hard shell. Its flesh is very soft and red as vermilion.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 52] On frogs
div.p: Frogs, Isidore says, are so named from their croaking (garrulitas), for they croak often, and this is a sign of fair weather; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "when the frogs in the mud have sung their old complaint." There are, Isidore says, many kinds of frogs: some are aquatic, living in the water and serving as prey to fish; some are marsh-dwellers; some are called rubetae, so named because they live only among thickets and briars, and these are, of all frogs, the greatest enemies of serpents. Others are called calamites, living among reed-stalks, small and green and voiceless, but very venomous: if the corpse of one of these is offered as food to dogs, they will become mute, without bark, and so such a morsel is called calamentum.

div.head: [II, 2, 4, 53] On sponges
div.p: The sponge is a kind of very tiny frog, Isidore says, named from a Greek word meaning "to cleanse" or "to wipe." This creature is proven to be living by the blood clinging to the rocks, for when the sponge is cut away from the stone, its blood remains on the rock where it was attached, and from this it is shown to be a living thing, even though it has no limbs nor any shape of a living creature. Hence some hold that sponges of this kind stand halfway between plants and animals. Their substance is useful for wiping and cleaning; whence Cicero: "and the blood was wiped away with sponges." Of sponges, Isidore says, some are male, having a thin body with narrow channels; others are female, with larger channels, and of these some are harder and hairier, having many pores, and are used for cleaning parchment. The very softest kind are called penicilli, and are suited for wiping the discharge from eyes and for treating swelling, by reason of their sponginess, which draws out harmful humours - for everything spongy draws things to itself by reason of its emptiness. The white, hard sponges used for cleaning parchment are made in this way: being naturally reddish and attached to rocks, they are cut away and spread out in the sun, where they are bleached white and hardened. Pliny, in his Natural History, names one hundred and forty-four kinds of all creatures living in water - sea-beasts and serpents, those common to land and water, fish, crabs, shellfish, lobsters, mussels, octopuses, soles, lizard-fish, squid and the like. The more notable among the authorities, however, are those that have been named here.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 1] General discourse on birds
div.p: After the walking creatures, which belong to the earth, and after the aquatic creatures, which belong to the water - though some of both kinds are amphibious, that is, living in both water and on land, as was said above - it remains, in the third place, to speak of the flying creatures, that is, the birds, which belong to the air. This order follows, as was said above, the degree of their familiarity to us: land creatures are most familiar to us and come first; then the aquatic; and last the flying creatures. For these, Isidore says, are the least known to us of all animals, as regards a sufficient account of their species, since, being far removed from human habitation, they dwell in deserts and uninhabitable places, namely in the wildernesses of India, Scythia and Ethiopia. The kinds of land animals are known to us through use and sight; the aquatic through sailing and fishing; but many kinds of flying creatures remain hidden in deserts and on the highest crags, Aristotle says, since, being inaccessible, they have never come to men's knowledge. The bird kind, Ambrose says, has flight by nature because it seeks its food not only on the ground, in a fixed place, but in the air, in no fixed place, and because it must often pass suddenly from place to place for its food, flight was necessary for it, being the swiftest kind of motion among animals that move from place to place. Ambrose says that birds use their wings in flying as we use our arms; with their tail, however, they steer themselves upward or downward in flight, and so, if a bird's tail is cut off, it can indeed still fly straight but cannot turn itself this way or that - and for this reason birds that need to swerve in flight, whether for hunting or for fleeing, have longer tails. Likewise no kind of bird, Ambrose says, lacks feet, and the necessity of this is that it seeks its living not only in the air but also on the ground; also, it could not always fly, owing to the fatigue of such motion; and also, having caught its prey or food in flight, it needed to hold it with its feet, and for this reason all the strength of birds that live by plunder lies chiefly in their feet and sinews. Of birds, Ambrose says, some live by plunder, and these have hooked claws on their feet for seizing prey, and curved beaks for tearing tough flesh more easily and quickly; others feed on fruits and seeds, and these have hollow, thick, soft beaks suited for gathering; still others live on varied, chance food, and these are of a disposition midway between the two. Also, birds of prey do not dwell together in flocks under a leader, since each would devour the other, whereas birds that are not predatory do dwell together in flocks under a leader. Also, some birds withdraw in winter and return in summer, as swallows; others always remain in the same places - the cause of this lies in the heat or cold of the places, and in the greater ease of obtaining food in a warm place than in a cold one. Also, some birds never grow tame, but always dwell in wild places; others do grow tame and take food from the hand; others still do not grow tame, yet always live in the company of men, as swallows do. There is also a difference among birds in voice and song: some delight in their song for its own sake, as the nightingale; some merely make noise, as geese; others learn words and human speech, as the parrot; some are chaste, as the turtledove; some incontinent, as the cock and the partridge; some vie in strength, others in beauty - whence Ambrose says that the cock is the more boastful, the peacock the more handsome. Also, some live alone, others only under a leader and in a flock, as cranes and storks. Also, some birds seek their food and living without plunder, on land, as crows, and these have broad, spread-out toes; others prey on fish in the water, and these have broad feet for swimming, so that they can be supported on the water, as geese and ducks, and these have long, broad beaks and a long neck, so that they can more easily catch fish and small twigs in the depths. Also, birds that nest in the water fly off when a storm comes, Ambrose says, seeking safer places or sweeter waters.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 2] On the eagle
div.p: The eagle, Isidore says, is so named from the keenness (acumen) of its eyes, that is, of its sight, because it sees most sharply. It is a great bird, king of all birds, and lives by plunder. It shuns the company of other birds, as the lion does among land creatures, and nests on the highest crags, where its nest cannot be found by man. Ambrose says it does this because greed always shuns the company of the many. Isidore says it sees so sharply that, flying so high as to be scarcely visible to man, it can look down and see the tiniest fish in the depths of the water or on the shore. When its young hatch from the egg in broad daylight, it holds them up by its talons against the sun, and whichever of them can bear the sun's light with a steady, unmoving gaze, it raises as its true offspring; whichever cannot bear it, it casts out as though a foreigner. The young it keeps, it guards and nourishes with great devotion, and once they are grown, it teaches them to fly and quickly casts them from the nest, since it becomes difficult to feed them further. As for the cast-out eaglets, unable to bear the sun's light, the osprey takes them in, joins them to its own young, and rears them.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 3] On the vulture
div.p: The vulture, Isidore says, takes its name from its slow flight, for it is a bird of great bulk and so cannot fly as swiftly as other birds of prey. Vultures have an excellent sense of smell, Isidore says, so keen that they detect corpses across the sea and follow after them, as eagles do too. Its bones are very resonant, and for this reason well suited to making pipes. Ambrose says vultures do not mate, but lay eggs without receiving any seed - though Aristotle says the contrary. Vultures live a hundred years and more, Ambrose says.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 4] On the bustard
div.p: The bustard (gradipes), Isidore says, is a bird as large in body as a ram, and cannot fly far, but runs mostly on its feet, whence it is named gradipes, "foot-walker." They live in level places, and gauge the distance of their range and pasture from the paths men take so as always to be able to take flight before an ambusher can reach them.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 5] On the crane
div.p: Cranes, Isidore says, take their name from the sound of their cry, since they seem to grunt in this way. These birds dwell together and fly together in a certain order, as if written in letters; whence Lucan: "and their scattered letter, with wings dispersed, is lost." They fly very high, so as more easily to see from afar which lands to make for, and to guard more easily against dangers around them. One of them leads the whole flock, going before, and urges on those following with a certain cry, and if she should grow hoarse, another takes her place. By night they divide the watch among themselves, and in turn, by rank, keep guard over the rest, holding small pebbles suspended between their claws so that they will not fall asleep, thereby warding off sleep. If they sense any danger, they at once cry out to warn their companions. One of them, Ambrose says, keeps watch over the rest, and when her turn of watching is done, she rouses another with a certain call, and then sleeps herself. Solinus says that cranes withdraw to the north in winter, and, so as not to be hindered by being driven back by contrary winds, they swallow sand. When about to cross the sea, they choose the narrowest crossing, and place small stones between their claws so as not to be hindered by the wind. When they are about to reach the shore, they drop these stones - and this has been confirmed, Solinus says, by sailors who saw the pebbles fall onto their ships. If one of them grows weary, all the others support and help her. They live long, Solinus says, and turn black as they grow old. They dwell chiefly around the river Strymon in Thrace during winter; whence Ovid: "and the Strymonian cranes," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 6] On the stork
div.p: Storks, Isidore says, are named from the sound of their bills, as though cyconiae, a sound they produce not with their voice but by clattering their bills together. These birds arrive at the start of spring, flying together like cranes, and are enemies of serpents, for they swallow whole any they find. The swallowed serpent, exiting again through the bird's rear, is taken up again and again by the stork, until at last, consumed by the heat of the stork's insides, it dies for good. Of which Virgil says in the Georgics: "the white bird comes, hateful to the long serpents." In wintertime they gather into a flock and travel to Asia, with crows as their leaders going before them. They show great devotion and care in tending their young, so much so that through their constant sitting on the nest they lose their own feathers, and when the parents grow old, their young repay them in turn, spending just as much time feeding and tending them. When they fly across lands, one of them leads the flock, guiding the course, another follows behind, driving on the rest. They avoid danger with such caution, Ambrose says, that they rarely settle to rest on the ground. Solinus says that upon their first arrival, the storks tear apart whichever of them arrived last. Storks have no tongue, the same author says, and for this reason have no voice by the office of mouth or tongue, but make their sound with the clattering of their bills, not by crying out.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 6, note 1] On storks and serpents
div.p: Wherever storks make their homes, it is deemed unfortunate and reckless to harm them, Solinus says. In Thessaly there is a great multitude of storks, the same author says, because serpents abound there, which the storks devour.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 6, note 2] On storks and purging
div.p: When storks feel themselves burdened by illness, they go to the sea and draw in seawater through the anus, and by then expelling that water again are purged - and from this the use of enemas was discovered by physicians.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 7] On the swan
div.p: The swan (olor), Isidore says, is the bird called in Greek cygnus. It is named olor from the Greek holon, "whole," because it is a bird entirely white. It is called cygnus from canere, "to sing," because it sings with a modulated voice, and this, Isidore says, is because it has a long, curving neck, and so produces high notes; and the sound comes out resonant, winding through the turns of its throat. Whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "but the goose honks amid the tuneful swans." It is said that in the year it is to die, it sings most sweetly, as if lamenting itself beforehand; whence Ovid: "so, when the fates call, cast down amid the wet grasses by the shallows of the Maeander, the white swan sings." In the Hyperborean regions there is a great multitude of swans, and when they hear the sound of lyre-players, they at once fly up and sing as if in contest with the players. Sailors always take the approach of this bird as a good omen, Isidore says; whence Aemilius: "the swan, among omens, is always the most joyful bird: sailors wish for it, because it does not sink beneath the waves." This same bird has very resonant bones.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 8] On the ostrich
div.p: The ostrich is a certain bird of Egypt, so called among the Greeks, and is, Isidore says, more a wild beast than a bird. It has feathers altogether like a heron's or a hawk's, and horse-like feet, and wide, prominent ears, but because of the size of its body it cannot fly. It is of so hot and moist a nature that it can even digest swallowed iron. It is so forgetful a bird that it leaves its eggs, laid in the sand, without brooding over them, and they are afterward brought to life by the sun's heat. It is cruel to its young, for it never broods over them, nor recognizes nor even seeks them out; whence it is said in Jeremiah: "the daughter of my people is become cruel, like the ostrich in the wilderness," and so on.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 9] On the heron
div.p: The heron is a certain bird, Isidore says, so named as though ardua, "lofty," because it flies very high; whence Lucan: "and the heron, daring to fly aloft." The reason it flies so high is that it greatly fears storms, and for this reason, when a storm threatens, it flees the clouds and betakes itself to higher altitudes; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "and the heron flies above the high cloud - this is a sign of a coming storm." This bird, Isidore says, is called by some authors the tantalus.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 10] On the phoenix
div.p: The phoenix is a certain bird found only in Arabia, and is so named, according to Isidore, because it has a phoeniceus, that is, a purplish-green colour - or else because it alone is unique of its kind, there being never more than one phoenix at any time; in the Arabic tongue, phoenix (fenis) means "one." It has a red breast in front, purple wings and other parts, and a green tail; yet over its whole body, against the light, it shows a greenish colour, from which it also takes its name. This bird lives five hundred years and more, and when the hour of its death approaches, it builds itself a kind of pyre of sweet-smelling wood and roots, and, sitting upon it, by beating its wings against the rays of the sun draws forth and kindles heat within itself, until, its feathers catching fire, it is wholly consumed together with the pyre. Then, on the third day, from the ashes of its burning a small worm is generated, which gradually, as feathers grow upon it, takes shape and is formed into a bird. The Observer says this bird is never seen by any curious man wishing to capture it, and nature provides for this because it alone is unique of its kind, and if it were captured or killed, that species would perish. Of this bird there is the verse: "in the lands of Arabia, fragrant with Sabaean incense, where that toilsome labour of place-names is born, there is ever but one bird, the phoenix," and so on. Solinus says that some have reckoned this bird's life to end with the completion of the Great Year, which some, the same author says, calculate at five hundred and forty years, others at twelve thousand, nine hundred and fifty-four years. The same author says that the phoenix once flew to Egypt and was caught there, and this is how it first became known.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 11] On the cinnamon-bird
div.p: The cinnamolgus, Isidore and Solinus say, is a certain bird found only in Arabia, like the phoenix. It is named from cinnamon, because it weaves its nests of cinnamon on the highest crags; and for this reason the men of that region, unable to climb up to its nests, shoot lead-weighted darts at them to bring down the cinnamon gathered there by the bird, which merchants especially seek and buy as being genuine and effective.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 12] On the parrot
div.p: The parrot, Isidore says, is a certain bird that dwells around the shores of the ocean among the Indians, entirely green, sometimes marked with a reddish colour, having a tongue broader than that of other birds, whence it learns to utter distinct words. By nature it has this trait, that it greets men; it learns other words, such as "hail" or "greetings," through use. Whence someone wrote to the emperor: "from you I, a parrot, shall learn the names of others: this alone have I learned to say on my own: 'Hail, Caesar.'" Solinus says this bird is entirely green, but has around its neck a reddish collar, and a beak so hard that, flying down from a height, it catches itself on the rocks with its beak alone; hence those who teach parrots to speak strike them on the beak with an iron rod as discipline. It also has a very hard, strong head. When it is young, it learns to speak words more readily; when old, it becomes incapable of learning. There are two kinds of them, one noble, the other common - and this is shown by the sinew of the toes in their claws, for the nobler kind have five toes, the common kind only three.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 13] On the halcyon (kingfisher)
div.p: The halcyon, Isidore says, is a certain bird named as though ales cyonea, "the sea-bird," because in winter it builds its nest on the pools of the ocean, betaking itself there to lay its eggs and rear its young. Whence, according to Virgil in the Georgics, a sign of fair weather is taken from the halcyon, because when it must brood over its young, there will then be seven continuous days of clear skies and calm seas; and for this reason those days are called by sailors the "halcyon days." Ambrose says that to the seven days in which it broods over its eggs it adds another seven for rearing its young, and during those days too the sea will likewise be calm; and this is what Virgil means in the Georgics when he says: "the halcyons, beloved of Thetis, spread their wings upon the shore."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 14] On the pelican
div.p: The pelican, Isidore says, is a certain bird that dwells only in the wildernesses and deserts of Egypt, around the shores of the river Nile; whence its name, pelicanus, "Egyptian bird," from the Greek pelos, "bird," and canopus, meaning the same as "Egypt." This bird, the naturalists say, kills its own young and mourns them for three days; then it wounds itself in the heart with its own beak and sprinkles its young with its blood, and so brings them back to life.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 15] On the strophades (harpies)
div.p: The strophades, Isidore says, are birds named after the Strophades Islands, where they alone exist and nowhere else; and according to some they are the same birds called, in the fables, harpies, whom Hercules overcame with his arrows. They are sea-birds dwelling on the Strophades Islands, and they lie in wait for passing ships, attacking the men aboard.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 16] On the crocodile-bird
div.p: The strophilus is a very small bird, Solinus says, and dwells only in Egypt, around the river Nile. It seeks its food in this way: it watches for when the crocodile, having devoured its prey, settles by the Nile's shore in the sun, and then the little bird approaches and settles in the crocodile's mouth, which it always keeps open, and picks out and eats the scraps of food still clinging between its teeth; and the crocodile does it no harm, since it delights greatly in having its teeth cleaned, something it could never otherwise manage - and so the little bird both feeds itself and does the crocodile a service.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 17] On the Diomedean birds
div.p: The Diomedean bird, Isidore says, is so named according to fable after the companions of Diomedes, who according to the story are said to have been transformed into these very birds. Whence it is said of them that if a Greek approaches them, they draw near and fawn upon him as if recognizing a fellow-citizen and companion; but if anyone else approaches, they attack him, and as if with tearful cries lament either their own transformation or the death of their leader Diomedes. These birds are found on the island of Diomedes, in Apulia, where Diomedes' tomb is; they resemble the coot in shape, are white in colour, with a long, broad, hard, red beak, and a body as large as a swan's, and they fly about the rocky sea-cliffs among the crags. The Latins call these birds Diomedean after the fable; the Greeks call them herons or coots. They have fiery eyes and see very sharply. Solinus says these birds have toothed beaks and fly together in flocks with two leaders, one going before to guide the course, another following behind, urging the rest on to greater speed. When they wish to breed, they dig hollows with their beaks and build a roof of wood above, cementing it with their own droppings. They make two openings in that nest, one facing east, by which they are roused in the morning and go out, another facing west, by which they return and enter at night. When weighed down by overeating, they wander here and there in flight to lighten themselves. They perform a kind of sacred rite, as if a sacrifice of some religion, every day, in this manner: they gather upon a certain rock, moisten their feathers, and sprinkle water over themselves, crying out and beating their wet feathers together, and so, the sacrifice as it were performed, return to their own places. This practice, Solinus says, gave rise to the fable that the companions of Diomedes were turned into birds. For Diomedes was killed on that island by the Illyrians; before Diomedes' arrival in Apulia, the island bore another name.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 18] On the Memnonian birds
div.p: The Memnonides, Isidore and Solinus say, are birds of Egypt, so named after Memnon, son of Tithonus, their reputed author, at whose tomb they gather every year according to the fable. Isidore and Solinus say that every fifth year they come to Troy and fly about there for two days, and on the third day tear at one another, fighting with beaks and claws, as if lamenting Memnon, according to the fable. The occasion for the fable is that, in historical fact, on the day Memnon was killed, many birds gathered even from the most distant regions to the Trojan corpses, and thereafter, whether every year or every fifth year, out of habit or drawn by the scent of corpses, they continued to do so.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 19] On the Hercynian birds
div.p: The Hercynian birds, Solinus says, are certain birds that dwell only in the forests of Germany, chiefly in the Hercynian Forest, whence they take their name. These little birds have feathers that glow so brightly by night that they give travellers light to find their way through that forest on dark nights.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 20] On the ibis
div.p: The ibis, Solinus says, is a certain bird dwelling in Egypt around the river Nile, shaped like a stork. When this bird feels weighed down, it purges itself by inserting its beak into its anus and injecting water. It preys upon serpents, taking their eggs and carrying them to its nest as food for its young. For this reason, Solinus says, the whole of Arabia and especially Egypt are kept free of serpents by these birds, and so it is forbidden for anyone to dare molest them there. They lay eggs through the mouth, Solinus says, though Aristotle disputes this, saying that no animal, as commoners suppose, can conceive or give birth through the mouth. Only the Pelusiac mouth of the Nile has a black ibis there; the rest are white. Josephus says that when the children of Israel were crossing the desert, Moses, because of the serpents there, had many ibises carried along with him in baskets, and released them where the serpents were, and the serpents were at once either devoured or driven off by them.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 21] On the bee-eater
div.p: The merops, Isidore says, is a certain bird, also called by the name gaulus. This bird shows such great devotion that it recognizes its own parents, and when they grow old, shelters and feeds them in its own nest.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 22] On the heart-eating bird
div.p: The coredulus, Isidore says, is a certain woodland bird, living on the corpses of dead animals, and of the whole body of a corpse it seeks the heart first to eat; whence it takes its name coredulus, as though "heart-eater."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 23] On the jackdaw
div.p: The jackdaw (monedula) is a black bird, Isidore says, named as though monetula, "little coin," for once tamed it is a playful bird that learns to utter distinct words through habit and training, and wherever it finds gold, or even coins, it steals them and buries and hides them in the earth; whence Cicero, in his speech for Valerius Flaccus, said: "gold should be entrusted to you no more than to a jackdaw." It is of a very hot temperament and suffers constant itching, especially on the head, and for this reason often seeks to have its head scratched.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 24] On the bat
div.p: The bat, Isidore says, takes its name from the fact that it flies only in the evening (vesper). It is amphibious: in the middle part of its body it is almost like a four-footed creature, resembling a mouse in nearly its whole body, and it has no feathers, but rather certain small membranes with which it flies. It is a creature hateful to birds and to all other four-footed animals alike, and for this reason it flies not by day but only by night, and more often in summer, for in winter it lies hidden. Its blood is warm, and is greatly sought by sorcerers for working various forms of trickery.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 25] On the nightingale
div.p: The nightingale is a small bird, of moderate size, Isidore says, and takes its name from the fact that at daybreak it announces, with its song, the light that is coming - for then it sings as if welcoming the approaching day. This bird is also called, by another name, acredula; of which Cicero says in his Prognostics: "and the acredula practises its morning songs."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 26] On the screech-owl
div.p: The ulula is a night-bird, Isidore says, so named because its voice imitates lamentation or groaning by its screeching (ululare). Whence augurs say that wherever this bird, present in a house, cries out, it signifies either fire or some other calamity; but when it is silent, this signifies good fortune. Whence Ovid: "Tisiphone, the wedding-attendant, screeched in that bridal chamber, and the ill-omened bird sang its mournful song."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 27] On the horned owl
div.p: The horned owl (bubo), likewise a night-bird, Isidore says, has a lean, modest body but is covered thick with feathers, a large head and great eyes, but its sight is dulled by day, though it sees better by night. It is hateful to all other birds, an ill-omened, foul and unclean bird, wandering by night and dwelling among men's tombs by day. Of which Ovid says: "and it becomes a foul bird, herald of coming grief, the sluggish horned owl, a dire omen to mortals."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 28] On the little owl
div.p: The little owl (noctua), Isidore says, is also a night-bird, much like the horned owl, but with this difference: it is smaller, and flies about the dwellings of men. This same bird is called nocticorax, "night-raven," for corax in Greek means "raven," and it is so named because it shuns the light and flies by night.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 29] On the screech-owl (strix)
div.p: The strix is likewise of the owl kind, Isidore says, a bird flying by night and making a sound resembling its own name - whence it takes its name from that sound. For when it cries out, it shrieks (stridet), and wherever it flies, it often foretells misfortune. Of which Lucan says: "what the fearful horned owl, what the night-screeching strix, lament."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 30] On the raven
div.p: The raven is called corax in Greek, and takes its name from the sound of its voice, since it croaks (crocitare) in a manner that its name echoes. Of which Virgil says in the Georgics: "and the ravens rejoicing with throaty cries." Isidore says that the raven does not feed its young well before they grow their feathers, because, owing to the dissimilarity in colour, it believes they are not its own; but once the feathers have come in and it sees them turn black, it then loves them dearly and feeds them abundantly. In every corpse, Solinus says, it goes first for the eye. When a raven flies croaking to its nest after rain, it is a sign of fair weather; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "it delights, once the rains have passed, to revisit its small brood and its sweet nest" - for during rain the raven is away from its nest, seeking food in the meantime. Whence the Psalm: "who gives food to the cattle, and to the young ravens that call upon him" - for meanwhile the young ravens live on rainwater alone.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 31] On the crow
div.p: The crow, Isidore says, is a bird of very great age, living a hundred years and more. Augurs say that crows love man and warn him, by their cries, of dangers to be avoided on the road, whether from the ambush of robbers or other perils. When crows fly together, it signifies fair weather; but when they scatter from one another with a certain cry, it signifies a storm - whence Virgil in the Georgics: "then the shameless crow calls for rain with her full-throated cry." Ambrose says that among the Latins the crow is called the "devoted" bird, because it shows such great devotion toward its young that it follows, guards and feeds them even once they are fully grown; and its parents, too, once they grow old, it likewise guards and feeds in turn, and when they can no longer fly, it lifts and supports them. If it sees another bird being pursued by a bird of prey, it flies to its aid and exposes itself to danger on the other's behalf. Whence, according to Ambrose, the crow has, as if by nature, won for itself that very reward - namely, long life - which is promised to those who honour their father and mother.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 32] On the chough
div.p: The chough (graculus), Isidore says, is a certain bird resembling the crow, so named because it constantly croaks (crocitare) and, in a manner of speaking, "chatters" (graculare) - not, as some think, because it flies in flocks (gregatim). It is a most talkative kind of bird, tiresome with its frequent cries.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 33] On the magpie
div.p: The magpie (pica), according to Isidore, is named as though poetica, "poetic," because it utters sounds distinctly, as man does; whence rustic poets too are called "magpies" among the authorities, and according to fable the Pierides were said to have been turned into magpies. It often betrays a man hiding in the woods, and is hostile to sparrows. It imitates the sound of man's voice with great effort; whence someone wrote: "I, the talking magpie, greet my master with a sure voice: if you did not see me, you would deny I am a bird."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 34] On the woodpecker
div.p: The woodpecker (picus), according to Isidore, is a bird similar in stature to the magpie, but marked with spots of green, white and black. This bird clings to trees with its feet and beak, striking often, and is named picus after Picus, son of Saturn, who often made use of this bird in his auguries. That this bird has a certain divinatory power and significance is proven by this: whatever tree it settles upon, that tree cannot long hold a nail or piece of iron driven into it, but as soon as the woodpecker settles on that same tree, the nail or iron falls out of its own accord, as it were. This bird is called the picus Martius, because augurs take from it signs of the outcomes of wars. The magpie, however, is a different bird from this one, contrary to what some hope.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 35] On the peacock
div.p: The peacock, Isidore says, is so named from the sound of its voice, for it has a harsh and frightful cry; and it is a bird whose feathers seem gilded and painted with every kind of colour, with a variety that not even royal purple can rival. The male is more beautiful than the female. It takes such great delight in the beauty of its own feathers that, when in darkness, it cries out, believing, since it cannot see itself, that it has thereby lost the beauty of its plumage. It walks with a subtle, stealthy gait, like a thief; whence someone wrote: "the peacock has the head of a serpent, the gait of a thief, the raiment of an angel, and the voice of a demon." It preys greatly upon serpents. Isidore says that peacock flesh is so tough that it can scarcely be cooked, and hardly ever putrefies; of this bird there is the verse: "you marvel, whenever it unfolds its jewelled wings, why, hard man, you could hand such a bird over to the cruel cook?"

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 36] On the pheasant
div.p: The pheasant, Isidore says, is so named after Phasis, an island of Greece, whence this bird was first brought to our lands; of this there is the verse: "first was I brought over on an Argive ship: before that, nothing was known of me but the Phasis." It belongs to the kind of wild fowl, and its flesh is very good to eat.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 37] On the cock
div.p: The cock, Isidore says, takes its name from castration, because among all other birds the cock alone is castrated; hence among the ancients too, castrated men were called "cocks." The female of this kind is called the hen (gallina), for pullus ("chick") is the general name for the young of all birds still immature, and sometimes even of four-footed creatures, as in the phrase "foal of an ass" (pullum asinae). Isidore says that a cock's limbs, mixed with molten gold, are consumed at once, so much so that they seem to pass into the very substance of the gold. Ambrose says: this bird is the herald of day, for it crows at daybreak; it walks alongside the hen and watches over her; if it finds anything on the dungheap, it calls her to it; it always keeps watch against birds of prey to guard its chicks. One cock suffices for many hens; if another cock arrives, they fight over the hens together, and whichever proves victor will claim the kingdom of the hens for himself. Hens, too, fight among themselves over the brooding of eggs; if one sits upon another's eggs, either there will be no offspring, or it will be malformed and deformed. The cock's boastfulness and courage lie in the crest on its head, in its spurs, its wings and its tail, which it always carries erect; whence Ambrose says: the cock is more boastful, the peacock more handsome. The Observer says that a cock, once it reaches nine years of age, lays an egg, which, if taken and brooded over by a toad, produces a basilisk.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 38] On the capon
div.p: The capon is a castrated cock. In its belly, after three years, is formed a precious stone called the allectorius, as is said in the Lapidary. This cock does not crow, does not breed, does not walk alongside the hen nor tend nor guard her, since it has lost the boastfulness it once had in its testicles; it does nothing but eat a great deal and readily fatten, and so is of no use except for the kitchen.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 39] On ducks
div.p: The duck (anas or aneta) takes its name, Isidore says, from its constant swimming (natare), for it swims often in the water, hunting fish and small twigs. Hence, Ambrose says, it has broad feet and toes, joined together by a kind of webbing, for the purpose of swimming, so as to strike the water, and a long, broad beak for catching fish; and for this reason it nests around still waters and marshes, where it more easily obtains its prey. Of this kind, Isidore says, some ducks are called "true" ducks (germanae), which are of better flesh, more nourishing and more easily digested.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 40] On geese
div.p: The goose (anser), Isidore says, takes its name from "duck" (aneta) by derivation, or from a resemblance to it, being like the duck, or because it too swims in the water like the duck. Geese, Isidore and Ambrose say, keep watch through the night and signal the coming day with a certain din and clamour. Hence the nighttime ascent of the Gauls onto the Capitoline Hill at Rome was betrayed by geese, and for this reason a golden goose was set up on the Tarpeian citadel of Rome and honoured by the people; whence Ambrose says: "Rome, you owe your rule to geese: your gods were sleeping, and the geese were watching. So on those days you sacrifice to the goose and not to Jove, and rightly do your gods yield to the geese, by whom they know they were then saved from being captured themselves by the enemy." Isidore says the goose has such a keen sense of smell that it detects the presence of men by scent alone, and even senses, through scent alone, the approach of day by night and in dark places. Whence someone wrote: "nor any less, in the darkness, does the goose - keen of scent, and clever with its blind honking - sense the dawn of day drawing near."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 41] On the coot
div.p: The coot (fulica), Isidore and Ambrose say, is a sea-bird named from the Greek lagos, "hare," because its flesh has the taste of hare's meat. It is a bird that nests in the middle of seas or lakes, on rocks surrounded on every side by water, and always delights in the depths. When storms threaten, it comes out of the water and moves about on the sands along the shore; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "and the coots play happily on the dry shore." That other fulica, however, which is called phoenix in Greek, is a mountain bird resembling the eagle, which rears the young or chicks cast out by the eagle; this is a different bird in kind, dwelling-place and role from the one described above, and it is these that we call "degenerate eagles."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 42] On the diving bird (merganser)
div.p: The mergus, Isidore says, is a certain bird so named from mergere, "to dive," because it often plunges itself, head first, into the water, and there senses a coming storm and flies at once, crying out, to the shore. Whence a sign of storms is taken from these birds; Virgil, in the Georgics: "when the swift divers fly back from the sea."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 43] On the hawk
div.p: The hawk (accipiter), Isidore says, takes its name from accipere, that is, "to seize" (rapere). More than other creatures that live by plunder, it is devoted to preying on other birds, and in its small body, Isidore says, it has such great strength that it will even attack hares and foxes when hungry, sometimes even at its own peril. Ambrose says this bird is unkind toward its young, for as soon as it senses they are able to fly, it drives them from the nest with bites and blows of its claws, and forces them to seek their own prey. All creatures that live by plunder do much the same, for, as Ambrose says, one who lives by the unjust lot of plunder can scarcely feed even himself. But of others it is said, by contrast: "you shall eat the labour of your hands: blessed are you, and it shall be well with you," that is, you shall have abundance; whence it follows: "your wife shall be like a fruitful vine," and so on. This law holds among men as much as among other animals.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 44] On the falcon
div.p: The capus, Isidore says, is a bird so named in Latin from capere, "to seize," which we call the falcon (falco), because it has curved toes shaped like a sickle (falx); hence it does not, like the hawk, seize its prey on the ground or in mid-air indiscriminately, but seeks its prey only in the air, swooping down upon flying birds from above and cutting them through the middle with its hind claw, which is stronger than the others, as if with a scythe. There are many kinds of falcons: the finest kind comes from the northern region, chiefly from Norway; these are as large as a goose or a swan, and white, marked with small black spots. When they fly out after prey, two always go together, so that while one flies above the birds to be preyed upon, the other drives them from below, and vice versa - for it captures its prey only by swooping down from above upon birds, and so it always strives to fly higher than the rest.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 45] On the kite
div.p: The kite (milvus), Isidore says, is numbered among the birds that live by plunder, and preys chiefly on domestic birds. Since it cannot, owing to the slowness and weakness of its strength and flight, pursue other birds, it takes its name from this very softness and feebleness of body and flight; for milvus is named, Isidore says, as though mollis, "soft."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 46] On the osprey (bone-breaker)
div.p: The ossifrage, Isidore says, is likewise a kind of bird that lives by plunder, a most voracious bird and of such great bulk that it hurls ibexes down from the highest crags and cliffs; and once it has devoured their flesh, it takes their bones and, flying very high, drops them down onto rocks so that they shatter, and then likewise eats their marrow - whence it is named ossifragus, "bone-breaker."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 47] On the turtledove
div.p: The turtledove takes its name, Isidore says, from the sound of its voice, and is a quiet, modest bird, always among crags and mountain ridges and remote wilderness, far from the dwellings of men - the opposite of the pigeon, which loves the roofs of men's houses and their company. Ambrose says this bird is so chaste that once it has lost its mate, it never again pairs with another, but mourns its widowhood and its loss.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 48] On the pigeon
div.p: The pigeon, according to Isidore, is so named because with every turn of its neck it changes colour, from the refraction of light rays upon its feathers, which are like a polished mirror; or else pigeons (columbae) are so called as though colentes lumbos, "cherishing the loins." They are so given over to love that they conceive through a kiss, and breed all year, in every month except the two months of the solstices. Isidore says pigeons have no gall bladder. Male pigeons fight among themselves over the females and over nesting places. In brooding, male and female take turns, though the female more often broods the eggs, except while she eats - at which hour the male even drives her from the nest by force, and himself broods the eggs meanwhile.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 49] On the wood-pigeon
div.p: Wood-pigeons (palumbes), according to Isidore, are named as though parcentes lumbis, "sparing the loins," for, contrary to the pigeon, they cherish chastity, and nest not in houses but in trees. Once they lose their mate, they never take another. These are called, among common folk, wild pigeons, and have a hoarse voice, continually as if moaning, in the trees where they perch; whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "nor meanwhile will the hoarse wood-pigeon, your care, nor the turtledove, cease to moan from the lofty elm."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 50] On the partridge
div.p: The partridge, Isidore says, is a woodland bird, so named from its cry, and it is a crafty and cunning bird, and so lustful that the male even mounts other males; and so deceitful that a female of this kind will steal another's eggs and brood them herself - yet once the chicks are grown, they recognize their true mother, who bore them, and go to her, abandoning the one who reared them by theft. They recognize one another by their calls. They are so curious that at the sight of some marvellous thing, or an unfamiliar colour, they fix their eyes upon it until they become entirely stupefied and forgetful of themselves; and for this reason fowlers carry before them a red cloth stretched on sticks, and drive the partridges, transfixed by the sight of it, into their nets. Solinus says that in Boeotia partridges keep, both on land and in the air, certain fixed bounds which they dare not cross, even though they are elsewhere free throughout the land. They build their nests of the sharpest thorn-twigs and cover them over with dust on the ground, so as to keep other birds or men from approaching. Female partridges hide their chicks from the males, because the males harm them with excessive ardour and attention. The females are so lustful that they conceive from the scent of the males alone. If a man approaches the nest where the partridge chicks are, the mother comes out and goes before him, feigning weakness and exhaustion, and does this with the intent of drawing the man away from the nest, never letting him come near her, and when the man tries to catch her, she suddenly flies off. When they sense they are seen by a man, they lift clods of earth with their feet and hide themselves in the dust so that they seem almost to vanish before his eyes. They dwell, with their nests, only among the densest thickets, never in open ground.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 51] On quails
div.p: Quails, Isidore says, are so named from the sound of their voice. The Greeks call them ortygiae, because they were first seen on the island of Ortygia. They have their fixed season for arriving, for in summer they cross the sea, and the one that leads their flock is called the ortygometra. When they draw near land, the hawk seizes them, and for this reason, for greater safety, they always choose a leader of another kind, better able to foresee dangers. They gladly eat the seeds of poisonous plants, and for this reason the ancients forbade their use as food. Isidore says that this creature alone, among animals, suffers from the falling sickness [epilepsy], as man does. Solinus says they cross the sea together in such great numbers that they sometimes sink ships, when, exhausted by night, they fall all together onto the ships' prows. They never set out when the south wind blows, for they fear being battered and worn out by the force of a stronger wind; for they are of a very plump body, and for this reason cross the sea only on a steady north wind.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 52] On the hoopoe
div.p: The hoopoe, Isidore says, is a small bird with a crested head and long feet. It is a foul and unclean bird, always dwelling among tombs and feeding on human dung.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 52, note] On the hoopoe's blood
div.p: Isidore says that if anyone, going to sleep at night, anoints himself with the hoopoe's blood, he will see demons suffocating him. Its blood is useful for the practices of enchanters and the arts of sorcerers.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 53] On the cuckoo
div.p: The cuckoo, Isidore says, is a bird that we call, by another name taken from the sound of its cry, cuculus. This bird is accustomed to settle only on dry branches, and cries "cuckoo" until the summer solstice. It is a very hot-natured bird, and for this reason often bathes in the coldest springs. This bird alone suffers from leprosy. It has fixed seasons for arriving, appearing only in summer, and when they fly in, they perch singly on the shoulders of kites and are carried by them, for they cannot fly well on their own. Isidore says that from the droppings of these birds, mixed with sage, summer cicadas are generated.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 54] On sparrows
div.p: Sparrows, Isidore says, are small birds, so named for their smallness, or from pascere, "to feed," because they eat often. This bird is exceedingly lustful, whence, as Aristotle says in his book On Life and Death, male sparrows have a shorter life than females. A sign of old age is that old sparrows have a black ring around their neck.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 55] On the blackbird
div.p: The blackbird (merula) was called in antiquity medula, Isidore says, because it sings sweetly (modulari); according to others, merula is named as though mera, "sole," or mere volans, "flying alone," for it flies not with companions but alone; or it is named merula as though merens, "grieving," because a certain kind of them, which fly along rivers, signal coming storms with their song. This bird, Solinus says, though black in every other region, is born white only in Achaia.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 56] On the nightingale (Philomena)
div.p: Philomena is a small bird that in summer sings most sweetly by night, so much so that she is thought to hatch her eggs no less by the sweetness of her song than by the warmth of her body. Whence the naturalists say that she broods over her egg for an hour, and then, standing on her right foot upon the egg, sings again. This little bird is much given over to love, and so delights in her own song, beyond the memory even of love or of the eggs she tends, that from the very excess of her singing her brain sometimes bursts and she dies; whence she is named philomena from the Greek philos, "love," and mene, "failing," as though "failing through love."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 57] On the swallow
div.p: The swallow, Isidore says, is so named as though aeriundo, "going through the air," because it does not take its food while sitting, but in going and flying through the air. It is a chattering bird, always flying about the roofs of men's houses and building its nest of mud and straw plastered against walls. It does not fly in a straight line but always in twists and turns. Because it cannot be caught, on account of this very trait, this little bird alone is never taken as prey by other birds - and not, as Solinus says, because it is held sacred and placed under the protection of some divine power. Swallows do not remain or nest, Solinus says, in a house about to collapse, but withdraw from it. They depart at the autumn equinox and fly across the sea; they return at the spring equinox. When swallows fly excitedly around ships on the water, it is a sign of a storm; whence Virgil in the Georgics: "or the chattering swallow flitted about the pools." In the belly or stomach of an old swallow is formed a precious stone called the celidonius. Ambrose says it nests in houses so that its young may not be harmed by birds of prey. When it builds its nest, it gathers twigs and straw with its beak, then flies to water and wets its feathers, and so, with wetted feathers, rolls itself in sticky mud, so that the mud clings to it, and thus carries the mud along with the straw to build up the nest. If its young happen to be blinded, it anoints their eyes with the juice of celandine and restores their sight.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 58] On thrushes
div.p: The thrush, a certain kind of small bird, Isidore says, is so named from its slowness (tarditas), for it is slow of flight. These birds appear in summer, but withdraw in winter. The turdella is a smaller kind of thrush. From its droppings the finest birdlime is made. In wintertime, upon their return to us, they are caught with birdlime. They are of pleasant flavour to eat.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 59] On the fig-eater (beccafico)
div.p: The ficedula, Isidore says, is a small bird of green colouring and a fine singer, so named because, fed on figs, it sings all the more gladly and sweetly. Whence the verse: "since I am nourished on figs, since I feed on sweet grapes, why did the grape not rather give me its name?"

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 60] On the goldfinch
div.p: The goldfinch (carduelus) is a small bird, most pleasing for its varied colours and its sweet song, and is so named, Isidore says, because it feeds on thistles (cardi) and thorns, and, fed on these, sings all the better. Hence among the Greeks this bird is also called athalantis, "from the thorns," on which it is nourished.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 61] On the bunting
div.p: The furfurio, Isidore says, is a certain kind of bird so named because it feeds on bran (furfur), grain ground into meal, and this is its food.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 62] On the onocrotalus
div.p: The onocrotalus, according to Isidore, is a general name for all birds having long beaks, and does not denote the species of any single bird. Concerning these birds a precept is given to the Jews in the Law.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 63] On the caristian birds
div.p: The Caristian birds, according to Solinus, are a certain kind of bird found only on the island of Crete called Carystus, whence they take their name. These birds fly through the midst of flames, and are in no way consumed by fire.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 64] On the griffin
div.p: There are also, among the flying creatures, some that have the shape of land animals along with feathered wings besides. Of all these, the largest bird - or rather beast - is the griffin. It is, Isidore says, a winged, four-footed animal, born in the Hyperborean mountains, resembling a lion in every part of its body, but with wings and a face like an eagle's, and it is so fierce a creature that it tears apart any men it sees. It is above all hostile to horses; whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "now shall griffins be yoked with horses," and so on - setting this down as an impossibility, since these creatures are natural enemies of one another.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 65] On the pegasus
div.p: The pegasus, Solinus says, is a certain bird found only in Ethiopia, having in every part of its body the shape of a bird, but with horse's ears alone - whence it took its name, for pegasos in Greek means "horse."

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 66] On the tragopan
div.p: The tragopan, similarly, Solinus says, is a bird found only in Ethiopia, larger in its whole body than an eagle, as birds go, but having on its head long, curved ram's horns.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 67] On augury
div.p: Augury, Varro says, is the foretelling of future events from the motion, gesture and flight of birds, and from their voice - a conjecture partly superstitious, partly probable. For some augury is superstitious, as the belief that magpies flying by signify a guest's arrival, since birds are in no way affected by that guest's coming, and so no true sign concerning such things, to which they are not attuned, can be drawn from them, whether truly or probably.
