Other augury, however, is natural and probable, since signs of the outcomes of those things to which birds are secretly attuned beforehand can, on this basis, be drawn from them - not with certainty, but probably. Such are the auguries Virgil describes in the first book of the Georgics, as he himself explains there in that passage: "I do not indeed believe that they have a divine intelligence," and so on. Augurs therefore distinguish, on this basis, three kinds of birds. Some are called, according to them, oscines, birds that give an omen of future events by mouth and song, as the raven, the crow, and the woodpecker. Others are called alites, which show future events by their flight, and these, if unfavourable, are called inhibiting signs - as in the line from the Bucolics: "often has the crow, from the unlucky holm-oak on the left, foretold misfortune." If favourable, they are then called prepetes, as though "seeking what lies ahead," as in the line: "the swan, among omens, is always the most joyful bird." The third kind is a common one, consisting of flight, motion, gesture and voice together.

div.head: [II, 2, 5, 68] On eggs
div.p: All kinds of birds lay eggs, Isidore says, and for this reason birds are born twice: first from their mother, second from the egg. The necessity of egg-laying in egg-laying creatures arises because, owing to a weakness of natural power, they cannot generate a fully-formed offspring within the womb, and because of the scarcity of nourishment in the womb - a scarcity caused by the great quantity that is diverted out into the generation of feathers. Eggs (ova) are so named as though "moist" (humida), because they are full of moisture within, and that moisture is of two kinds: one, from which the chick is generated, and this is the yolk; the other, by which the chick is fed and nourished within the egg, and this is the white. For the generative and the nutritive powers work together from the very beginning of conception, Aristotle says. Among eggs, the better ones are those which, it is observed, are white, elongated, and fresh - these have the finer flavour. Some eggs are fertile eggs, produced by mating; others are "wind-eggs," from which no chicks come, so called because the female conceives them not through mating but through the scent of the male. It is the nature of eggs, Isidore says, that wood soaked in a fresh egg cannot be made to burn. Eggs mixed with quicklime also glue together broken pieces of glass, the same author says. The nourishment of eggs is reversible, physicians say, being wholesome for the healthy but harmful for the sick.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 1] On the tiny flying creatures, in general
div.p: "Tiny flying creatures" is a term used by the authorities for two reasons: either because they are smaller than all those named above and do not lay eggs but mate, as bees do, or because they are born from putrefied matter without mating, as beetles and flies, as was likewise the case among land creatures. Ants and worms are called "tiny" for the same reason, or simply because they are smaller in bodily size. All tiny creatures, when they fly, are heard to buzz, as it were, and this for two reasons, Aristotle says in his book On Sleep and Waking: first, because of the striking of the outer air, though this effect is weak in tiny creatures; and second, and more importantly, because of the drawing in of the offending [buzzing] sound toward the whole covering membrane by which they fly - for in tiny flying creatures, properly speaking, one does not call them "feathers" or "wings," but rather the whole membranous covering with which they fly.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 2] On bees
div.p: Bees are the foremost and noblest kind of the tiny flying creatures. They are named, according to Isidore, either because they bind themselves together, foot to foot, or because they are born without feet, in the manner of a little worm, and only afterward gradually acquire feet and wings. Many naturalists say much about their nature and usefulness. In sum, their nature is this: they are diligent in the task of making honey. They build their dwellings from the coarser matter of flowers, and construct many cells, which they arrange among themselves in order, and produce countless offspring. They keep an ordered camp and a king; they wage war against foreign bees, stinging and fighting with their stingers, and once a bee has lost its sting, it dies. Their king alone has no sting; he is larger in body than the rest, and, according to Aristotle, he alone breeds. Ambrose and Isidore say the contrary of this. Bees die from smoke, and are frightened by noise and commotion. Virgil, in the fourth book of the Georgics, says that bees can be artificially generated from the putrefied flesh of oxen or calves, just as hornets are generated from horses, drones from mules, and wasps from donkeys. Avicenna gives the reason why bees' honey is better than Attic honey: Attic bees merely carry the substance of flowers and do not further concoct it in the mouth, whereas true bees transform and, in a sense, cook the honey in their mouths, and for this reason their honey is purer and better - just as wheat, once chewed, ripens an abscess, but unchewed wheat will not do this. The "castri," Isidore says, are those bees that dwell at the outer edges of the honeycombs, and these are called "kings" (reges) because they lead the encampment (castra).

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 3] On the drone
div.p: The drone (fucus) is larger than the bee but smaller than the hornet, and is born from the flesh of mules; it is named fucus, as though focus, "hearth," Isidore says, because it consumes the labour of others. Of which Virgil says: "it wards the idle drones, a lazy herd, from the hives."

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 4] On wasps
div.p: Wasps are born from the flesh of donkeys. They have large stingers and a head so hard that it can scarcely be crushed.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 5] On hornets
div.p: Hornets are generated from the flesh of horses, and from these in turn are generated beetles, whence they take their name [scarabei, from scabrones].

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 6] On the buprestis
div.p: The buprestis is named as though "crushing oxen" (boves premens). It is a kind of flying creature found in Italy, resembling a beetle, with long legs. It hides among the grasses, and when cattle graze there, it bites them with the tube of its mouth and so inflames them that their gall bladder bursts and they die.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 7] On the glow-worm
div.p: The glow-worm (cicendela) is named as though scintilla, "spark," and is a kind of flying creature that flies by night during the dog days and glows in the darkness like a spark. Whence the verse: "and they scatter like sparks in a reed-bed," that is, like glow-worms.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 8] On the cockroach
div.p: The cockroach (blatta) is a kind of flying creature so named from its colour, for when caught it even stains the captor's fingers with its dark hue. This creature flees the light, whence it is called lucifuga, "light-fleeing," and is the opposite of the fly, which loves the light, and is for this reason also called lucipeta, "light-seeking."

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 9] On butterflies
div.p: Butterflies are flying creatures that fly about chiefly in summer, when mallows are in flower. From their droppings are generated the worms of vegetables and leaves.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 10] On locusts
div.p: The locust, according to Isidore, is so named because it has long legs like a spear-shaft (hasta), and there are two kinds, a sea-locust and a land-locust, both of which the Greeks name from "spear" as hastago. These, Ambrose says, devour crops and scorch them with their bite. The bird called in Greek the seleucus preys on them and devours them.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 11] On cicadas
div.p: Cicadas, Isidore says, are born from the spittle of cuckoos, and are a kind of flying creature that sings ceaselessly in the height of summer heat. Whence Virgil in the Bucolics: "beneath the burning sun the groves resound with cicadas." Though these creatures are mute nowhere else, Solinus says that among the Reginans in Italy they are silent.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 12] On flies
div.p: The fly, Isidore says, comes from a Greek word. Flies are born in summer, from heat and putrefaction, and when they are numerous, it is a sign of pestilence in the air that year. Flies drowned in water come back to life again after a while.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 13] On the dog-fly
div.p: The cynomia, Greek for "dog-fly," is a large fly born from the putrid flesh of dogs.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 14] On the gnat
div.p: The gnat (culex) is named from its sting (aculeus). It has in its mouth a tube with which it pierces the flesh and sucks blood.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 15] On the scymphes
div.p: The scymphes, Isidore says, are very tiny flies, but more troublesome than others because of their stronger and larger stings.

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 16] On the gadfly
div.p: The gadfly (oestrus) is a flying creature harmful to herds of cattle, and is a Greek word; in Latin it is called asilus, and commonly the horsefly (tabanus).

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 17] On the fruit-fly (vinegar fly)
div.p: The bibiones are tiny flying creatures born in must (fermenting grape juice), which some call mustiones, from mustum, "must." Whence Afranius says: "when you wait for me and begin to chatter, fruit-flies fly out of your mouth into your own eyes."

div.head: [II, 2, 6, 18] On the weevil
div.p: The weevil (gurgulio) is a kind of extremely tiny flying creature, so named because almost none of its parts are visible except its throat (guttur).
